The PS5 is on everyone's list right now thanks to the juggernaut release of GTA 6, but finding a console can be tricky. Now that PS5 Black Friday deals are live, I'll be tracking price drops across Amazon, Walmart, Best Buy, Target, GameStop, and, of course, PlayStation Direct.
Beyond the consoles themselves, I'll also be watching for the best savings on accessories and games. In fact, you can already get PS5 games starting from as little as $9 . So now's the time to upgrade your library ahead of the holidays.
One last thing: you can grab a brand-new PS5 DualSense controller for just $54 at Amazon right now . With gaming prices skyrocketing this year, a 28% saving on Sony's excellent pad is well worth taking advantage of.
We'll keep this page updated throughout the day, so bookmark it and follow along. And if you’re looking for a big screen to play your PS5 on, check out our Black Friday TV deals live blog . Now, here are the best Black Friday PS5 deals you can buy right now.
PlayStation's best-selling driving simulation series takes realism to a whole new level in this seventh mainline installment. The power of the PS5 is fully utilized by Gran Turismo 7 to bring players an authentic driving experience that is practically unparalleled. Plus, the game now packs full PSVR 2 support via a free in-game update.
Ratchet & Clank: Rift Apart sees PlayStation's iconic intergalactic mascots go on their wildest adventure yet. Both Ratchet and Clank are playable, as well as a brand new character, Rivet. The game plays in gorgeous 4K at 60 fps thanks to the power of the PS5, and really takes advantage of the console's full next-gen capabilities.
If the full-price release of The Last Of Us Part 1 put you off the idea of retracing Ellie and Joel's steps in this gorgeous remake of one of PlayStation's most well-known titles, now's your chance to pick it up. The remake features improved visuals, new animation work and more tactical, more aggressive enemies, making exploring the post-apocalyptic USA all the more stressful, and all the more engaging.
Housemarque's challenging, procedurally generated third-person roguelike shooter is still one of the PS5's best games, and if you've yet to play it, it's a bargain at this price. The game sees you taking the reins as Selene Vassos, a pilot who crash-lands on an ever-changing world home to tons of dangerous alien lifeforms. Equip yourself with strange weapons and abilities and explore the ever-changing map one loop at a time.
Stellar Blade is a hack-and-slash action-adventure game in the best spirit of the genre. It takes full advantage of the PS5's horsepower and serves up thrilling combat sequences and an engaging story. The graphics aren't half bad-looking, either.
Control Resonant surpasses its excellent predecessor thanks to its larger scope, both narratively and gameplay-wise. The melee-based combat is appropriately brutal and engaging, while the various skill trees offer a deep level of customization.
Long before Elden Ring, Bloodborne and Dark Souls, From Software released Demon's Souls , the first Souls title to truly establish the core gameplay loop that has taken the gaming world by storm. For the current generation, Sony had Bluepoint develop this faithful, beautiful remaster, which improves on the original title and updates it with amazing graphics, new weapons, and items.
Sony’s standard PS5 pad remains one of the best controllers around thanks to its responsive haptic feedback and adaptive triggers. Standard colorways, including white, midnight black, cosmic red, and galactic purple, are down to $54 here, beating PlayStation Direct’s sale price.
The Razer Raiju V3 Pro's TMR sticks offer precise control over movements while removing the risk of stick drift, and the gamepad’s Hall Effect triggers are fantastic too. The controller is highly customizable with removable back buttons and personalization via Windows and/or mobile software.
The PS5 is hard to come by this Black Friday, and if you do find one, it's at retail. That stings, but it doesn't hurt to get a PS5 when you can. This model is the base PS5 Slim, now the cheapest PS5 available. It comes with an 825GB SSD.
The PlayStation Portal is a great way to stream your PS5 games while on the go. Right now, Walmart is selling a bundle for the streaming handheld for $35 off. The bundle comes with the PS Portal, a carrying case, a protective sleeve, a charging station, and wired earbuds. This is an overall great bundle.
One of our favorite pro-style PS5 controllers just fell to an all-time low. Right now, you can get the Turtle Beach Victrix Pro BFG reloaded for $129 at Amazon . That's $80 off its normal price and the lowest it's ever been on sale for. In our Turtle Beach Victrix Pro BFG Reloaded review , we praised its very responsive Hall Effect triggers and thumbsticks and its long battery life.
Just like many of you, I'm currently playing through GTA 6 and instead of using a DualSense controller, I'm using the Victrix Pro BFG reloaded. Sure, I am missing out on Sony's haptics but this controller's remappable buttons make playing the game a breeze. Plus, the Victrix Pro BFG is very ergonomic and hasn't let me down yet, even during long, extended play sessions.
When it comes to Star Wars games on PS5, most people will wax lyrical about Galactic Racer or Jedi Survivor, and don't get me wrong, both deserve their flowers, they're great games, but so is Star Wars Zero Company. Don't let it be forgotten!
Now on sale for $44 on Amazon , in this turn-based tactics game, you control the titular squad, a scrappy group of mercs and misfits, roped into a dangerous mission with high stakes. I'm not usually one for tactics games, but Zero Company really hooked me at launch because of its accessible combat design and its focus on player choice. If you play with "permadeath" switched on (and you should), squad members can die for good in battle, which means every decision you make feels important. There's a wealth of content and loads of ways to customize your team.
It's not just the PS5 Pro suffering from stock issues this holiday season; the regular PS5 is also becoming very tough to find at MSRP. The likes of Amazon, Best Buy, and Walmart are sold out, but at GameStop, you can get a PS5 Slim Digital Edition for $599 (aka its regular price). Meanwhile, if you're okay with a refurbished model , you can get a refurbished PS5 starting from $499 over on PlayStation Direct .
Dragon Quest is one of the most beloved JRPG series, but it's nowhere near as popular as Final Fantasy, at least in North America. If you'd like to experience the first three games with fancy new graphics, you can buy both HD-2D versions at a Black Friday discount. Pro-tip: play Dragon Quest III first, since it's canonically the first game, then Dragon Quest I and II.
Pragmata is a brand-new IP from Capcom and one of the most interesting games I've ever played. Instead of just shooting enemies until they expire, you must first disable their shields via a puzzle mini-game. This makes each encounter feel more intense, since you have to solve the puzzle before you get overwhelmed. Capcom delivered an exceptional experience.
In case you missed our previous post, the DualSense controller is now $54 for Black Friday. You can get this official PS5 controller in a slew of colors, so you don't have to compromise on the exact controller you want. I always have spare controllers just in case, and I suggest you do, too.

articles.title_orig: Ted Cruz Blames China for Data Center Water Fears: ‘You’re Being Lied To’
articles.title_zh: Ted Cruz Blames China for Data Center Water Fears: ‘You’re Being Lied To’
articles.content_orig:
Republican Senator Ted Cruz of Texas said Friday that China is funding influence campaigns to convince Americans that artificial intelligence data centers consume excessive amounts of water, calling such concerns "false" and part of a broader effort to slow the nation's technological development.
Speaking on his Verdict podcast with political commentator Ben Ferguson, Cruz alleged that China-backed operations have rapidly shifted public opinion against data centers to gain an advantage in the global race for AI dominance.
"If you're worried data centers are stealing your water, you're being lied to. That is a false argument," Cruz said. "China is paying money to convince you [that] you should be scared."
Newsweek reached out to Cruz's office and the Chinese Embassy for comment by email.
Texas has become a central battleground over AI infrastructure due to its available land, energy resources and business-friendly regulatory climate. State officials and technology firms have promoted the multibillion-dollar investments as vital to economic growth and national competitiveness.
The Lone Star State is one of the nation's largest and fastest-growing data center markets, with more than 400 facilities operating statewide as of September 2025, according to the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). The research organization estimates that existing Texas data centers consume about 25 billion gallons of water annually for direct cooling and electricity generation, a figure projected to rise as AI development accelerates.
At the same time, disputes over water demand, electricity consumption, local control and environmental impacts have grown increasingly prominent in state politics.
Kathryn Guerra, the Dallas-based campaign director for Public Citizen's TCEQ Watchdog program, told Newsweek that Cruz is out of touch with what's happening in Texas communities.
"Gaslighting Texans about water concerns isn’t going to help, but what could have helped is transparency around water consumption–something state leadership failed to ensure," she said. "Texans deserve clear answers about how much water data centers will consume, their water source and how regulators will enforce limits. Until companies are compelled to report water data with real penalties for non-compliance, Texans will remain unconvinced."
Cruz said on Friday that China views AI as a strategic competition with the United States and benefits when Americans oppose data center construction.
"China and America are in a race for AI," he said. "If you're [Chinese President] Xi [Jinping] in China, the single best way to win this race is convince America handcuff themselves, tie their hands, stop developing AI, surrender, and let China win," the senator said.
According to Ferguson, foreign influence campaigns have played a major role in turning the public against the facilities, particularly by amplifying concerns over water usage.
"We've found out not that long ago that there [were] hundreds of thousands of bots that were basically putting misinformation, scare tactics in the marketplace to turn people away from data centers," he said. "That was all, by the way, being paid for by China."
Cruz added: "The number one and number two argument against data centers: number one, water. You need to understand if you're worried data centers are stealing your water, you're being lied to."
He maintained that newer facilities increasingly rely on closed-loop or air-cooling systems that require minimal water.
"Almost every data center going in uses either what's called closed-loop cooling, which means the same water gets circulated round and round and round, so it uses almost no water," Cruz said. "So almost every data center uses less water than a golf course."
Most analysts continue to view the United States as the overall leader in frontier AI development.
American companies including OpenAI, Anthropic, Google DeepMind and Meta operate many of the world's most advanced AI models and attract the largest private-sector investment. President Donald Trump has repeatedly cited this lead, saying the U.S. is "leading China" in AI.
But the gap may be narrowing as China's rapid advances, particularly following the emergence of Chinese AI firms such as DeepSeek, have raised concerns among U.S. policymakers and industry leaders.
China is producing competitive AI models, expanding domestic chip development and investing heavily in AI research and deployment. A growing share of top AI researchers are now based in China, and Chinese companies have become major players in generative AI, robotics and industrial applications.
China's government has also made AI leadership a strategic national priority, with Chinese President Xi previously calling for a global AI governance framework while simultaneously encouraging domestic innovation and deployment.
The debate about data centers escalated during Texas' 2026 gubernatorial campaign. In September, outgoing Republican Governor Greg Abbott ordered a moratorium on data center approvals, barring the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) from issuing new permits while collecting additional operational data from tech companies.
“Simply put, Texans must come first. Data centers must pay their own way, protect our grid and water and complete the ERCOT [Electric Reliability Council of Texas] and TWDB [Texas Water Development Board] audits. Until they do, TCEQ will issue no permits sought by data center projects," Abbott said in a statement.
The freeze marked a shift from earlier in Abbott's tenure, when he called Texas “the epicenter of AI development,” adding: “We must ensure that America remains at the forefront of the AI revolution, and Texas is the place where that can happen.”
Democratic Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa repeatedly criticized the industry's rapid expansion during her campaign, arguing the state lacked adequate oversight. At a campaign event in Amarillo, she described the boom as "the wild west of data centers."
"They are owned by the richest men in the world. We're all footing the bill. There are no rules. It is the wild west of data centers," she said.
Hinojosa pledged in an October video posted on X to maintain a statewide halt on new projects until lawmakers enact stricter regulations.
"When I am governor, I will issue a moratorium, a ban, on all data center approvals until laws can be passed by the Legislature to protect Texans," she said.
Earlier this month on Fox News, the governor-elect elaborated on her proposal, stating that economic development and stronger regulations could coexist.
"I don't hate data centers. I hate the way they're taking advantage of Texans. We don't have laws to protect Texans. We need a ban on new data center permits until we can pass laws to protect Texans and most importantly, and so Texans can have a seat at the table to decide if and how data centers come into their communities."
Earlier this month, the governor notified TCEQ that it could resume reviewing and issuing data center permits after ERCOT had finished gathering information on potential community impacts for its upcoming audit report, according to the Houston Chronicle.
The decision cleared the way for several major developments, including permits tied to SpaceX's proposed supercomputing facility and gas-fired power plant near Boca Chica, a CloudBurst project near San Marcos and an Atlas Energy Solutions project near Abilene.
Cruz's remarks come as researchers and environmental advocates warn that water demand tied to data center growth poses a significant planning challenge for the state.

articles.title_orig: US Chip Rental Rule Slows China's AI Labs, Beijing Calls In the National Team to Prop Up Stocks
articles.title_zh: US Chip Rental Rule Slows China's AI Labs, Beijing Calls In the National Team to Prop Up Stocks
articles.content_orig:
Chinese stocks rebounded sharply on Friday after a rare intraday state media readout cheered investors as top policymakers pledged to expand the role of state-backed funds in supporting the market.
The STAR index surged 14%, led by Chinese chipmakers such as CXMT , Cambricon and SMIC. The CSI Semiconductor index of 40 chip stocks climbed by 17.6% in its biggest single-day gain on record, surpassing the prior record of nearly 17% in late 2024, according to Wind Information.
The gains were widespread across mainland and Hong Kong stock indexes. The Hang Seng index rose 2%, while the CSI 300 index climbed 4%, its biggest jump since October 2024, according to Wind data.
The rally comes as governments pour support into domestic chip industries while tightening controls on sensitive technology in the global race for artificial intelligence.
The U.S. unveiled a new rule last week to further restrict Chinese companies’ access to advanced AI chips, including through overseas data centers, adding pressure on Beijing to accelerate its push for semiconductor self-sufficiency.
Friday's rally comes after the CSI 300 on Thursday sank to its lowest level since the escalation of the U.S.-China tariff war in the spring of 2025, according to Wind data.
In recent months, investors have weighed the commercial feasibility of Chinese artificial intelligence developers and tighter U.S. restrictions on advanced chips.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang oversaw a meeting Friday morning of the State Council, the country's top governing body, which saw officials pledge to strengthen the role of "National Team" — referring to state-backed funds — to stabilize markets and ensure ample liquidity, according to a readout released by state media Xinhua News.
The explicit reference to the "national team" is a first for a State Council meeting, said Bob Chen, a Shanghai-based venture capitalist and economist.
Authorities also stressed that "capital markets are crucial to the broader economy," according to the readout, a rare comment from a government that has not always looked favorably on the financial sector.
"Stock market performance is now prioritized at the highest level for the Chinese government," which is boosting investor confidence, Chen said.
"That's very strong language from the top officials," said Zong Ke, a portfolio manager at a Shanghai-based quantitative fund.
By Ke's calculations, stock trading volumes surged rapidly after the readout was released around 1:00 p.m. local time (12:00 a.m. ET). Full-day turnover across the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing exchanges was 52% higher than the previous session.
Policymakers also vowed to strengthen the role of "stabilization funds" like Central Huijin Investment, a state-owned investment firm that holds equity stakes on behalf of the State Council.
That message "effectively institutionalized Central Huijin's role as a state stabilization fund," said Hong Hao, managing partner of Lotus Asset Management. "And it's significantly positive news for the market."
Hao expects this market rally to prove more durable than the "fleeting bounce" triggered by Beijing's stimulus talks in the past, which wore off in days. "This time it's for real."
The readout of the Cabinet's meeting, typically released well after trading hours, was published around noon local time during trading hours, an unusual timing that's viewed by markets as a bullish signal.
The State Council also pledged better policies to steer medium- or long-term funds, such as insurance and social security funds, into equities, and encouraged listed companies to pay more dividends and step up share buybacks, while vowing a crackdown on financial fraud to protect investors.
The national team will accelerate asset purchases, Ke said, adding that he expects more supportive policies to follow, such as further loosening the institutional constraints that have limited long-term funds from investing in stocks.
Beijing's reliance on intervention to offset stock volatility has, however, raised questions about the market's ability to sustain longer-term gains.
But the market needs this kind of support right now, said Ke, as the near-term aim is to ease liquidity pressure and restore confidence so the market doesn't fall much further.
Chinese AI-related stocks also carry less downside risk than their U.S. counterparts, as the companies have spent less on AI so far and their shares have already been through a sharp correction, Ke said.
That, together with the pledged state backing, has given investors more confidence that the market may be nearing its bottom, Ke added.

articles.title_orig: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
articles.title_zh: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
articles.content_orig:
China's economic might is drowning out our voices, say activists and dissidents
For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.
"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."
It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.
But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.
It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .
But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".
Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades
Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls , Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.
China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power , drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.
Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times.
Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust.
The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles.
Sheznhen, a rich, buzzing city on the soth-eastern coast, has emerged as one of China's star attractions for tech and tourism
China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society.
"At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities."
China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation.
This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build.
In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded.
His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields.
That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response.
"Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says.
Donald Trump and Xi Jinping have held three summits so far this year
Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time".
The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? "We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas."
Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services.
"China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added.
These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms.
In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January.
Consul-General Wei Xiaodong (in the red scarf) pictured sending people off in January
"He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page.
Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say.
The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang.
"People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says.
Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope.
Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China.
"She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," says Alim.
"The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political."
Xinjiang has been sold as an exotic destination, bringing in huge numbers of tourists
When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity.
The Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial".
"It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says.
"Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable."
These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say.
Abduweli Ay

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Russian military flotilla bound for Libya turns around after warship sunk on November 22, sources say
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Russian military flotilla bound for Libya turns around after warship sunk on November 22, sources say
articles.content_orig:
By TOM COTTERILL, DEPUTY DEFENCE AND FOREIGN AFFAIRS EDITOR
Published: 08:49 EST, 27 November 2026 | Updated: 12:30 EST, 27 November 2026
Giorgia Meloni has publicly rebuked Ukraine for sinking a Russian warship in Libya and insisted the war 'cannot spread to the Mediterranean'.
The Italian prime minister issued the statement after Volodymyr Zelensky confirmed on Monday that suicide drones had destroyed the Merkury at a port in Benghazi.
The £150million corvette, one of the Kremlin's newest warships, was crippled on Sunday after two drones slammed into its hull and exploded.
Kyiv 's assault also targeted a sanctioned Russian cargo vessel, which was struck off the Libyan coast by a drone packed with explosives.
Mr Zelensky hailed the operation as an 'exemplary' demonstration of Ukraine's growing ability to punish Moscow 's assets wherever they may be.
But the mission triggered dismay in Italy , which considers the Mediterranean as part of its strategic backyard, with Ms Meloni fearing the war could now spill out into the region.
'The war must not, cannot spread to the Mediterranean,' she said at a European summit. 'We must be very clear on this – as we have been in recent days with our Ukrainian friends.'
The comments come at a time when Ms Meloni faces mounting resistance domestically over Rome's support for Kyiv, with the strikes threatening to become a fresh thorn in her side.
Italian prime minister Giorgia Meloni has rebuked Ukraine for sinking a Russian warship in Libya
The £150million corvette Merkury missile ship was engulfed in flames after a blast rocked the Libyan port of Benghazi
The destruction of the ship presents a major loss to Putin's navy, which has suffered repeated attacks since the invasion of Ukraine
Italy's firebrand deputy prime minister Matteo Salvini, the hard-Right leader of the League party, is an admirer of Vladimir Putin and is seeking to slash aid to Kyiv. He was fiercely critical of the attacks in Libya.
His party said in a statement: 'Conducting military operations on the territory of a sovereign nation without prior consultation with western partners – who have supported Ukraine economically and militarily for years, and particularly with Italy, which holds significant strategic interests in Libya – is unacceptable.'
Kyiv defended its right to hit Russian ships, even those docked in Benghazi, hundreds of miles away from the battlefield.
However, Italian foreign minister Antonio Tajani branded the Merkury's sinking as 'worrying'. 'It was a mistake to violate Libya's sovereignty,' he said, adding: 'Italy was absolutely unaware of Kyiv's intentions to strike in Libyan territorial waters, even inside a port.
'If this is a continuation of the war between Russia and Ukraine, just a few hundred kilometres from Italy, this is worrying, especially because we work for the stability of Libya.'
Libya is often a staging post for migrants seeking to enter Europe. It is split between two rival factions, with the west run by the UN-recognised administration in Tripoli, led by prime minister Abdul Hamid Dbeibeh, and the east controlled by the Libyan Arab Armed Forces leader Khalifa Haftar.
Ms Meloni has expressed her dismay to Volodymyr Zelensky over the attack in the Mediterranean
A Ukrainian Sea Baby drone is seen charging towards the sanctioned Russian cargo ship Angara off the Libyan coast on Sunday
Mr Haftar is an ally of Putin and previously attended Moscow's 'Victory Day' parade marking the Soviet Union's part in defeating Nazi Germany in the Second World War.
The Kremlin is also understood to be seeking to use Libya as a new military outpost to refuel and resupply its ships after abandoning the Tartus naval base in Syria.
Ms Meloni has already made it clear she has no intention of slashing Rome's support for Kyiv as a result of the attack but has expressed her deep concerns about Libya to Ukraine.
'I think we must do our best to continue helping Ukraine to defend itself, but we must also defend the security of our borders and our citizens,' she said. 'On this, I have been, and will continue to be, very clear with President Zelensky.'

articles.title_orig: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
articles.title_zh: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
articles.content_orig:
Spain's main party leaders have held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez saying he is confident of defying the polls.
"I cannot imagine us losing," he said, posing for selfies with supporters in red T-shirts and accusing conservative rival Alberto Núñez Feijóo of planning a coalition with the far right.
Feijóo's People's Party (PP) is narrowly ahead in the polls, and in the final hours of the campaign he travelled first to Barcelona and then Seville, promising voters a new political era of "truth, decency and good governance".
He accused Sánchez of evading questions on key issues like corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt.
The Socialist leader heads one of Europe's few left-wing governments, and with the French presidential elections five months away, there is a real chance that two of the continent's biggest economies could move to the right in quick succession.
Almost 39 million people have a vote in Spain and while commentators expect a high turnout, most polls have suggested a close finish. Under Spanish electoral law, no polls have been published since Monday.
"This time, yes, we're going to do it," Feijóo told PP supporters, in a nod to his failure to form a government three years ago despite winning most seats.
If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took place in front of thousands of people in a bull-ring in Valencia on Spain's east coast.
The venue was filled with Spanish flags and green Vox banners, and one of the biggest cheers of the night came when the secretary general of the party called for "less burka and less halal".
Ignacio Garriga said he was not acting out of hatred but love for the homeland.
A small section of the crowd could be heard chanting "Viva Franco" in reference to the dictator, whose death in 1975 heralded the start of Spain's transition to democracy.
A number of first-time voters at the rally said they were supporting Vox because of its policies on immigration.
Lledó, 18, said what had happened in Ceuta in the summer, when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory from Morocco, showed Sánchez was not able to control the country's border.
She had come to the bullring with her mum and aunt, Carli Chilet, who argued that Vox "are the best for women's rights".
Vox is hoping to almost double its seats from the 33 it won three years ago. It backs policies such as "national priority" - putting Spanish citizens first for welfare - and "remigration" for foreigners not considered to be contributing to the economy.
The final day of campaigning was very much in the shadow of a four-way TV debate the night before that exposed Spain's sharply polarised politics.
All four leaders had solutions for the housing crisis. Feijóo said the PP would build a million homes over four years, while Sánchez said housing should be a right not an object of speculation and profit.
While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, Sánchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front), focused on women's rights.
The two leaders seized on a moment in the debate when the PP leader accused Colau and the rest of the left of staying quiet during a flood disaster in Valencia, briefly moving his finger to his lips. The word he used "calladita" is a diminutive and can also be used to tell a woman to "keep quiet" in a condescending manner.
Sánchez reacted immediately and called on him to show "a little respect", accusing him of sexism.
Feijóo sought to clarify what he meant on Friday, and accused Ada Colau of remaining silent during "these years of corruption". His decision to wind up his campaign in Seville was significant, because the wider southern region of Andalusia has 61 seats in Spain's 350-seat parliament, more than any other.
Andalusia is also important because it is run by a coalition made up of the PP and Abascal's Vox, as are three other regions, Extremadura, Aragón, and Castilla y León.
Feijóo has insisted he wants to govern with a majority, backed up by "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox and says he has never spoken to Abascal about giving Vox ministerial power.
"Governing is about managing, and I have spent my whole life preparing for this moment," he said in Seville.
One of his new supporters at the rally was a retired woman called Isabel who told Spanish public broadvaster RTVE that she was attending a PP rally for the first time. The formerly loyal Socialist voter said she was "disillusioned" with a party led by  Sánchez. Another voter at the rally said Spain needed "a good manager".
Sánchez took to the stage in Madrid with his wife Begoña Gómez, and donned a red T-shirt that read "power of the people".
He then went on to praise Colau and her left-wing coalition's campaign.
"These elections are about moving Spain forward, not taking it backwards," he said.
Socialist supporter Leon Felipe, 25, told Reuters news agency: "Well, I think what's at stake in these elections is a big deal, is not a change of government... but rather a return to the past - a return to Franco's dictatorship.
"So, I believe that young must mobilise."
As he was speaking, Colau told a large audience in the south of Madrid that not only would they "not remain silent, we will win", vowing to form another "progressive government".

articles.title_orig: Gold and Silver Jump as Beijing Vows to Support China's Stock Market
articles.title_zh: Gold and Silver Jump as Beijing Vows to Support China's Stock Market
articles.content_orig:
Chinese stocks rebounded sharply on Friday after a rare intraday state media readout cheered investors as top policymakers pledged to expand the role of state-backed funds in supporting the market.
The STAR index surged 14%, led by Chinese chipmakers such as CXMT , Cambricon and SMIC. The CSI Semiconductor index of 40 chip stocks climbed by 17.6% in its biggest single-day gain on record, surpassing the prior record of nearly 17% in late 2024, according to Wind Information.
The gains were widespread across mainland and Hong Kong stock indexes. The Hang Seng index rose 2%, while the CSI 300 index climbed 4%, its biggest jump since October 2024, according to Wind data.
The rally comes as governments pour support into domestic chip industries while tightening controls on sensitive technology in the global race for artificial intelligence.
The U.S. unveiled a new rule last week to further restrict Chinese companies’ access to advanced AI chips, including through overseas data centers, adding pressure on Beijing to accelerate its push for semiconductor self-sufficiency.
Friday's rally comes after the CSI 300 on Thursday sank to its lowest level since the escalation of the U.S.-China tariff war in the spring of 2025, according to Wind data.
In recent months, investors have weighed the commercial feasibility of Chinese artificial intelligence developers and tighter U.S. restrictions on advanced chips.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang oversaw a meeting Friday morning of the State Council, the country's top governing body, which saw officials pledge to strengthen the role of "National Team" — referring to state-backed funds — to stabilize markets and ensure ample liquidity, according to a readout released by state media Xinhua News.
The explicit reference to the "national team" is a first for a State Council meeting, said Bob Chen, a Shanghai-based venture capitalist and economist.
Authorities also stressed that "capital markets are crucial to the broader economy," according to the readout, a rare comment from a government that has not always looked favorably on the financial sector.
"Stock market performance is now prioritized at the highest level for the Chinese government," which is boosting investor confidence, Chen said.
"That's very strong language from the top officials," said Zong Ke, a portfolio manager at a Shanghai-based quantitative fund.
By Ke's calculations, stock trading volumes surged rapidly after the readout was released around 1:00 p.m. local time (12:00 a.m. ET). Full-day turnover across the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing exchanges was 52% higher than the previous session.
Policymakers also vowed to strengthen the role of "stabilization funds" like Central Huijin Investment, a state-owned investment firm that holds equity stakes on behalf of the State Council.
That message "effectively institutionalized Central Huijin's role as a state stabilization fund," said Hong Hao, managing partner of Lotus Asset Management. "And it's significantly positive news for the market."
Hao expects this market rally to prove more durable than the "fleeting bounce" triggered by Beijing's stimulus talks in the past, which wore off in days. "This time it's for real."
The readout of the Cabinet's meeting, typically released well after trading hours, was published around noon local time during trading hours, an unusual timing that's viewed by markets as a bullish signal.
The State Council also pledged better policies to steer medium- or long-term funds, such as insurance and social security funds, into equities, and encouraged listed companies to pay more dividends and step up share buybacks, while vowing a crackdown on financial fraud to protect investors.
The national team will accelerate asset purchases, Ke said, adding that he expects more supportive policies to follow, such as further loosening the institutional constraints that have limited long-term funds from investing in stocks.
Beijing's reliance on intervention to offset stock volatility has, however, raised questions about the market's ability to sustain longer-term gains.
But the market needs this kind of support right now, said Ke, as the near-term aim is to ease liquidity pressure and restore confidence so the market doesn't fall much further.
Chinese AI-related stocks also carry less downside risk than their U.S. counterparts, as the companies have spent less on AI so far and their shares have already been through a sharp correction, Ke said.
That, together with the pledged state backing, has given investors more confidence that the market may be nearing its bottom, Ke added.

articles.title_orig: S&P cuts France outlook to negative
articles.title_zh: S&P cuts France outlook to negative
articles.content_orig:
Bearish dynamics remain contained in European rates despite the ECB’s tightening bias and firmer energy prices. French spreads tightened ahead of S&P’s review, but political uncertainty and budget risks could warrant a negative outlook – and keep investors cautious
Left on their own with the US out on holiday, European rates briefly tested the upside. While the European Central Bank accounts clearly pointed to the ECB’s tightening bias – maybe even beyond December – and energy prices also sneaked higher as tensions in the Middle East continue to simmer, a bearish dynamic failed to take hold in the end. What lingers is the uncertainty around the tech narrative.
French bond spreads did manage to tighten over the past session, taking the 10y spread over Bunds below the 150bp threshold.
This seems to defy the risk of S&P lowering the outlook on the stable A+ rating it currently still attaches to France. Given the uncertain political backdrop, further budget slippage over the year and an eroding growth outlook, S&P may have enough reason to do just that. At the same time, it would no longer really come as a surprise. Fitch lowered the outlook of its A+ rating to negative at the end of October in an unscheduled move after having only just reviewed the country in August.
Moreover, markets are already pricing France more like a BBB-rated country. To be fair, much of this is likely an overshoot. In its recent Financial Stability Review, the ECB pointed to the procyclical role of hedge funds in eurozone government bond spread dynamics. At the same time, the lingering threat of a downgrade might create another hurdle for investors looking to return to the French bond market.
The Bank of England has reiterated its intention to introduce measures to strengthen the gilt repo market, which could negatively impact demand for gilts. Hedge funds have acted as an important marginal buyer over the past year, helping absorb the significant increase in gilt supply. A popular strategy is buying cash gilts and offsetting these positions with shorts in gilt futures, whereby repo markets offer the ability to leverage up such trades. The slight pricing difference between cash gilts and gilt futures can provide attractive returns. But if the repo costs were to rise, the attractiveness of such trades could fall.
In effect, hedge funds offer balance sheet capacity to house gilts, and therefore any headwinds to such trades can add upward pressure to gilt yields. But the impact is more nuanced. Because the gilt positions are hedged through futures, any unwind of the hedge fund positions should be relatively neutral in terms of term premium. We would, however, expect gilts to underperform swaps. The spread between swaps and gilts is strongly linked to the balance sheet costs of holding bonds. If hedge funds decide a trade is no longer attractive due to higher trading costs, then other players with higher balance sheet costs (such as banks) would have to jump in.
We will see preliminary inflation data for November in France and Spain, where headline rates are expected to ease somewhat but remain at elevated levels. The ECB will also publish its consumer survey on expected inflation. ECB officials scheduled to speak are Chief Economist Philip Lane, Vice President Boris Vujčić, Germany's Joachim Nagel and France's Emmanuel Moulin.
In primary markets, Italy will auction 5y and 10y BTPS as well as 8y and 9y CCTeu floaters (in total up to 8bn).

articles.title_orig: Kyiv offers Black Sea ceasefire to protect grain exports
articles.title_zh: Kyiv offers Black Sea ceasefire to protect grain exports
articles.content_orig:
Ukraine has presented a proposal for a possible ceasefire in the Black Sea, as Kyiv seeks to protect its grain exports amid escalating attacks on shipping and port infrastructure.
Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha announced the proposal on Friday during the “Food from Ukraine” conference, saying Kyiv was ready to restore freedom of navigation and ensure the uninterrupted export of agricultural products.
“We are now awaiting a response from Russia. All of our proposals have been conveyed,” Sybiha said.
Moscow has sought to include oil transportation in the proposed ceasefire deal, but the Ukrainians say that issue belongs in a broader energy ceasefire.
He accused Russia of repeatedly putting forward “unrealistic demands” in response to Kyiv’s proposals, according to Suspilne, Ukraine’s national broadcaster.
The latest ceasefire initiative comes amid growing international concern over the security of commercial shipping and global food supplies. Ukraine and Russia are both major agricultural exporters , and attacks on vessels and port infrastructure have disrupted shipments transiting through the Black Sea.
A previous UN- and Turkiye-brokered agreement allowed Ukrainian grain exports to resume following Russia’s full-scale invasion in February 2022.
However, Moscow withdrew from the arrangement in July 2023, prompting Kyiv to establish an alternative maritime export corridor.
In August, Reuters reported that Ukraine had conveyed an earlier proposal through a third party for both sides to halt attacks on civilian targets in the Black Sea. At the time, Ukrainian grain exports had fallen 76 percent year-on-year, as shipowners avoided ports in the Odesa region following repeated Russian strikes.
International efforts to secure a limited ceasefire have since gained traction.
On October 31, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said Washington was reviewing proposals from Turkiye and India to facilitate uninterrupted grain and energy shipments.
The diplomatic impasse also comes as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy voiced his frustrations with US President Donald Trump’s approach to Moscow.
In an interview with the BBC on Friday, Zelenskyy criticised Trump for describing Russian President Vladimir Putin as “my friend” following their meeting in China last week.
“It’s strange. He is an aggressor and a killer. He can’t be a friend. Just cannot be,” Zelenskyy said.
He also criticised Washington for what he described as excessive neutrality in its dealings with Moscow, arguing that the US should use its influence to pressure Russia into meaningful negotiations.
“When you try to be very neutral with the aggressor … it means you support victims and you support also aggressor. It’s not right,” he said.
After talks in Florida on Wednesday, the NATO Secretary-General Mark Rutte called on Russia to avoid actions that could expand the war and urged a peaceful resolution as soon as possible.
Rutte has also stressed that any eventual peace agreement or long-term ceasefire must include security guarantees for Ukraine.

articles.title_orig: U.S. military says it disabled another ship that tried to breach naval blockade on Iranian ports
articles.title_zh: U.S. military says it disabled another ship that tried to breach naval blockade on Iranian ports
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. military has disabled a merchant ship in the Gulf of Oman that was trying to run its blockade of Iranian ports, U.S. Central Command said Friday.
A military aircraft fired "precision munitions" at the stern of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer on Thursday, and the "ship's propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed," it said in a statement.
According to U.S. Central Command, the Pacific Archer left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas before it attempted to run the blockade. Ship tracking websites list the vessel's destination as Singapore.
The commander of the Iranian navy, Shahram Irani, said Friday on state television that Iran will carry out operations "that will not only break the naval blockade but also drive the enemy out of the region's waters."
The strike comes as the Trump administration weighs its options in the long-simmering war with Iran, which began at the end of February and has settled into a quiet stalemate in the past several months.
Earlier in November, officials in the region told The Associated Press that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was pushing the U.S. to restart the war or allow Israel to launch airstrikes on Iran's nuclear facilities and missile capabilities.
Meanwhile, government and security officials from the Persian Gulf countries, as well as Pakistan and Turkey, were engaged in a diplomatic campaign, which included phone calls with senior U.S. officials, to stave off a renewed war in the region.
President Donald Trump has oscillated between threatening additional large-scale strikes on Iran and insisting that the war "militarily is effectively over."
The U.S. military has maintained a sizable naval force in the region, including a constant presence of two aircraft carriers and a host of other ships.
The U.S. has been blockading Iranian ports since April, though the blockade was lifted in the summer during talks with Tehran and resumed in July. Since then, the U.S. military says it has redirected 158 merchant ships and disabling those that refuse to comply.
The Pacific Archer is at least the 15th disclosed vessel to be disabled by the U.S. military since the blockade began in the spring and the sixth since it resumed this summer. The previous vessel was disabled on Nov. 7.
In June, the practice drew condemnation when a military strike on a Guinea-Bissau-flagged tanker attempting to evade the American blockade resulted in three deaths.
Three Indian sailors were killed when American forces struck the Palau-flagged M/T Settebello, officials in India said at the time. The leader of the International Maritime Organization, a United Nations agency, condemned the attack.
U.S. Central Command has consistently said that American forces issue multiple warnings before firing on the merchant ships.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard said on Friday that two tankers attempted to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an "unauthorized" route, claiming that one of them struck a naval mine while the other was forced to turn back.
The claims could not be independently verified.
In a statement carried by Iran's state broadcaster, the country's Revolutionary Guard also said the number of oil tankers attempting to transit through unauthorized routes in the critical waterway has sharply decreased in recent days.
Iran continues to warn ships not to pass through the strategic shipping lane without approval from Tehran.
Oil flows in the first two weeks of November fell by around 20% to around 13 million barrels per day compared with October, when exports roughly equaled the prewar amounts of 15-16 million barrels per day, according to Rystad Energy.
Reasons for the November decline include Iranian attacks that discourage tankers from attempting the strait crossing and reduced flows through a key Saudi pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, which has also been attacked several times.
A report by U.N. Trade and Development finds that disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the Black Sea and the Panama Canal are lengthening voyages, raising fuel costs, driving port congestion and adding to uncertainty. Alternative ports, inland transport and logistics arrangements have kept trade moving, but at a higher cost.
Toqa Ezzidin in Cairo contributed.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: Hackers breach US Air Force flagship Cloud One computing platform
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: Hackers breach US Air Force flagship Cloud One computing platform
articles.content_orig:
Hackers penetrated the Air Force’s cloud computing platform in a breach that could have exposed sensitive military information, a U.S. official said Friday.
The official confirmed the hack to NBC News but could not  provide any additional information about timing or the attack’s impact.
“The department of the Air Force does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities, or operational status of specific networks and systems,” an Air Force spokesperson said.
Reuters first reported about this most recent cyberintrusion against federal assets.
The FBI’s National Crime Information Center — which is used by federal, state and local authorities to share important information — was recently breached, sources briefed on the matter told NBC News this week .
And about two months ago, the FBI and Dutch national police arrested leaders of a “global cybercrime and threat actor group” that allegedly stole employee information from a bureau database. It is unclear whether any of these breaches are related.
“We continuously take prudent measures to protect department information, systems, and mission capabilities,” the Air Force spokesperson said Friday. “Ensuring the security, resilience, and availability of our most critical war fighting assets remains a top priority.”
“The department continues to assess and modernize its enterprise cloud capabilities to meet, evolving mission, security, resilience, and user requirements,” the statement continued. “Decisions regarding technical architecture, workload placement, contracts, and future capabilities are made through established governance, acquisition, and risk management processes.”
Courtney Kube is a correspondent covering national security and the military for the NBC News Investigative Unit.
Gordon Lubold is a national security reporter for NBC News.

articles.title_orig: Millions lose access to benefits and pensions services after 'cyber incident'
articles.title_zh: Millions lose access to benefits and pensions services after 'cyber incident'
articles.content_orig:
Millions of people have been left without access to online benefits and pensions services after the government said its system had been hit by a "cyber incident".
Downing Street has not ruled out an attempted hack but said there was "currently no evidence" personal data had been lost, adding an investigation was ongoing.
The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) said it took the digital services down as a "precaution", and assured claimants regular benefit and pension payments would be paid.
But a number of benefits recipients say money they rely on has still not come through - and they fear being penalised for not being able to fill in an online journal that proves they are looking for jobs.
The UK's former Chief Technology Officer David Knott told BBC Newsnight his "strong suspicion" was that the incident was an attack.
"They've taken down some of the citizen-facing services which implies to me that there's some kind of attack could be mounted through the front door," he said.
Single Cardiff mother-of-four Samantha Reah told the BBC the technological disruption meant she was missing £1,600: "I rely on the payment today - it's my payday.
"I have just enough money in my account to do a food shop. I'm panicking - it's going to be a long and stressful weekend."
Georgina Howarth, 30, from Plymouth, said she had to ask her mother for money to help buy food after not receiving her universal credit payment.
"I've been on the phone to them [DWP staff] every hour since 8am. They said they can't even get on the system."
Claimants are also unable to fill in an online journal which shows the DWP they have been applying for jobs, a condition of their benefits.
Gemma Barnes from St Neots in Cambridgeshire told the BBC she was worried her payments could be cut as a result.
She said she has been trying to access the universal credit website "all of today and since last night as well" but she has not been able to get through to the site.
"With it being so close to Christmas I need [that money] at the moment," she said., explaining she has to often rely on items in the reduced food section to make ends meet.
The DWP says regular payments are not affected and if customers have any issues with their payments, they should call on their benefit phoneline. They say they will not be sanctioned over missing journal entries during the incident.
There are also problems with Healthy Start, an NHS scheme for women who are pregnant or have young children to help them buy milk or fruit.
A spokesperson told the BBC the online application service was unavailable but there was no interruption to payments.
As of around 12:00 GMT on Friday, the online systems for pensions, universal credit and Pip applications, as well as the "Tell Us Once'" system to inform government when someone has died, could not be accessed.
It was not clear when the government expected services to be up and running again.
A DWP spokesperson said: "We are working closely with the National Cyber Security Centre and Government Cyber Coordination Centre to investigate and to bring services back online as quickly as possible and to minimise any disruption."
A statement continued: "As always, we will never message you to ask for bank details or ask you to click on links."
Tech disruption to major service around the world have hit the headlines repeatedly in recent months.
There was a major outage of Microsoft services, the grounding of all US flights, problems at the US National Security Agency, and disruption at major American banks.
The causes of these incidents have varied. Many were linked to upgrades going wrong but experts have also mentioned factors including outdated IT systems and the use of AI to potentially exploit tech vulnerabilities.
While the nature of the DWP incident is unclear, officials could not rule out the involvement of a "malicious actor", but added there was "no evidence" that other government departments had been targeted in this way.
The DWP outage follows warnings that AI technology could fuel attacks on UK digital infrastructure.
Earlier this month a National Cyber Security Centre report urged organisations to strengthen their defences against hackers as the technology becomes more complex and capable.
Its CEO Richard Horne said there was a "real prospect of an unprecedented rise in the number of cyber incidents".
Last month the government carried out inspections on several websites after a flaw was identified in a programming language used around the world .
The PHP security flaw prompted a global race for organisations to identify whether they were impacted and fix it before it could be exploited.
UK government websites have been impacted by other cyber incidents in recent years.
In April 2025, the government reported that cyber attackers had breached the Legal Aid Agency's online services.
It said the group responsible accessed a "significant amount" of personal data going back decades, including contact details of people who had applied for legal aid.
The agency took some services offline while responding to the incident.

articles.title_orig: Canada’s Supreme Court largely upholds a Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
articles.title_zh: Canada’s Supreme Court largely upholds a Quebec ban on religious symbols for public servants
articles.content_orig:
Canada 's Supreme Court has upheld Quebec 's controversial ban on Muslim headscarves and other religious symbols for certain public sector workers in a landmark ruling that reinforces the powers of provincial legislatures to override certain constitutional rights.
Six of seven judges concluded on Friday that Quebec had validly invoked the notwithstanding clause to protect the legislation, known as Bill 21, from certain constitutional challenges, in a significant victory for the province's separatist government.
The decision means public school teachers, police officers and government lawyers in Quebec will continue to face restrictions on wearing religious symbols while performing their duties.
However, the court unanimously ruled that a separate provision requiring elected members of Quebec's National Assembly to perform their duties with their faces uncovered violated their constitutional democratic rights.
The Supreme Court decision on Bill 21 is good news for Quebec secularism, but there was an unwelcome surprise in the ruling in the form of a loss of autonomy for the provinces in the way the Constitution’s notwithstanding clause works, Premier Paul St-Pierre Plamondon said Friday.
“We can be happy there is no setback on laicity as of today, but we can’t close our eyes to the fact there is a setback in terms of autonomy,” St-Pierre Plamondon told reporters.
“It’s a good day for secularism in Quebec, but the rules of the game have just changed without any political discussion with the provinces.”
Newsweek breaks down what the judgment and case mean.
At the heart of the legal battle is Section 33 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, known as the notwithstanding clause, which allows Canada's Parliament and provincial legislatures to override certain constitutional protections for renewable periods of up to five years.
The Supreme Court reaffirmed its interpretation of the provision dating back to a 1988 case involving Quebec's French-language laws.
The court said in its official summary that the exercise of the override power was “not subject to any limit other than those expressly set out in the provision’s text".
However, four of the seven judges concluded that courts retain the authority to determine whether legislation infringes constitutional rights even when governments have invoked the notwithstanding clause.
The court's summary said this power stems from "the principle of the separation of powers and the inherent jurisdiction of the judiciary to determine the legal effect of legislation and to grant a remedy".
No such declaration was issued in relation to the constitutional protections overridden by the notwithstanding clause, however.
Passed in June 2019 under former Quebec Premier François Legault, Bill 21 prohibits certain public officials in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols, including Muslim hijabs, Sikh turbans, Jewish kippahs and Christian crosses.
Some employees who already held their positions when the legislation was introduced are exempt from the restrictions under grandfathering provisions, subject to certain conditions.
However, opponents argue that the restrictions disproportionately discriminate against Muslim women, effectively forcing some to choose between their religious beliefs and their careers.
The legislation was challenged by teachers, religious organizations and civil liberties groups, including the English Montreal School Board, the National Council of Canadian Muslims and the Canadian Civil Liberties Association.
The case reached Canada's Supreme Court after Quebec's Court of Appeal upheld most of the legislation in February 2024.
Ewan Sauves, spokesperson for Legault, welcomed the ruling, describing it as "a historic decision that confirms Quebec’s right to make its own choices".
“Excellent news for the secular nature of the state and Quebec’s autonomy (and that of the provinces),” he said on behalf of the Coalition Avenir Québec politician.
The Supreme Court rejected arguments that Bill 21 could be overturned under constitutional provisions guaranteeing equal rights and freedoms to men and women.
Its official summary said Section 28 of the Canadian Charter “alone does not create a distinct right that could be invoked to challenge a law".
The court also rejected a challenge concerning the educational rights of Quebec's English-speaking minority.
The ruling confirms that teachers at Quebec's English-language public schools are subject to the ban on religious symbols, despite arguments that the legislation infringes the constitutional rights of the province's English-speaking minority to manage its own educational institutions.
The court acknowledged that the legislation could restrict English-language school boards' ability to recruit, retain, transfer or promote employees.
However, it concluded that opponents had failed to demonstrate that these restrictions undermined the “specific linguistic or cultural interests of the English-speaking minority” protected by the Constitution.
The court also upheld an earlier finding that the Quebec government's count of employees wearing religious symbols did not violate the Charter.
The English Montreal School Board (EMSB), which spent more than C$1 million ($702,940 USD) challenging the legislation in the courts, expressed disappointment at the ruling but vowed to continue its fight.
“We stood for vulnerable and marginalized people and I think we taught a good lesson to our students that everybody matters and we fought the good fight and you can't put a price tag on that,” EMSB president Joe Ortona said.
The Canadian Muslim Forum warned that the ruling would have “far-reaching implications for equality, faith freedom, women’s rights, and the future protection of fundamental rights in Quebec".
“The implications of this ruling extend beyond those directly affected today,” the organization said in a statement.
It added: “A society committed to equality and democracy must protect the rights of all its citizens, not make access to employment and public opportunities conditional upon abandoning deeply held beliefs.”
World Sikh Organization of Canada President Danish Singh compared Bill 21 to Canada's discriminatory immigration laws that led to the rejection of the Komagata Maru in 1914, noting that it took more than a century for Canada to apologize.
“We believe Bill 21 will also be remembered as a grave injustice. The people being harmed by it deserve action from their government today,” he said.
“We will never accept being treated as second-class citizens because of our faith. Sikhs and other religious minorities are entitled to full and equal participation in public life in Quebec and across Canada.”
James L. Turk, director of the Centre for Free Expression at Toronto Metropolitan University, told Newsweek he was “deeply disappointed” by the judgment but welcomed the decision to preserve the courts' ability to declare legislation incompatible with constitutional rights even when governments invoke the notwithstanding clause. “That's the one piece of good news in this decision,” he said.
Asked about the implications for the United States, Turk said the ruling “points to a weakness in the protection of fundamental human rights under the Canadian Charter,” but cautioned that Americans should not assume their constitutional protections were superior. “Fundamental rights in the U.S. Constitution, starting with the First Amendment, have been overridden through much of American history,” he said.
“What this shows to Americans is the weakness in the Canadian arrangements, but those same weaknesses happen in a very different way under the American Constitution,” Turk added. He argued that constitutional protections alone were insufficient, saying it was “only through political action, advocacy, protests, and so on, that we can protect our basic rights.”
All seven judges ruled against Quebec's government for attempting to enforce face-covering restrictions

articles.title_orig: Los Angeles schools block Google’s AI features, consider dropping tech giant’s products
articles.title_zh: Los Angeles schools block Google’s AI features, consider dropping tech giant’s products
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
Los Angeles school officials have blocked most student access to the artificial intelligence function embedded in Google’s widely used search tool — a milestone in enforcing the district’s AI moratorium and a direct rebuff of a new Google policy, but one that may prove temporary.
The AI block comes after Google announced that it would not provide a way for schools to block the AI overview that appears with its searches. At this point, company officials said, AI has become integral to the search function. If schools want the search function, they therefore have to accept that AI will come with it.
The policy prompted a national outcry among many educators and some politicians who said Google is forcing AI on children at a time when educators wants to place limits on the technology over safety and learning concerns.
In Los Angeles Unified, student access was blocked by a filter provided to the district by a company other than Google. District officials have neither released the name of that company nor provided details about how the action was accomplished. It applies to the AI overview that is displayed when a user enters a Google search prompt.
There also is a separate search option — called AI mode — that allows a deeper dive into AI. This feature already had been disabled on school-district computers provided to students.
“Google’s AI overview was temporarily suspended,” according to a statement provided by L.A. Unified. “Though we have an open dialogue with Google, they did not play a role in these recent improvements... Temporarily suspending Google’s AI Overviews is part of the District’s ongoing efforts to manage students’ access to emerging technologies and ensure their online experiences are age-appropriate and safe.”
L.A. Unified provided limited detail about its AI block in response to repeated queries, and there was no public announcement. At the staff level, at least, the nation’s second-largest school system appears to have no interest in going to war with Google or even calling attention to what some parents view as a significant accomplishment.
“LAUSD successfully exercised their power as a public school district over this corporation’s attempt to control its AI policy,” said district parent Bridie Lee, a leader within the group Schools Beyond Screens. She added that members of that group “fought back against Google issuing this ultimatum and the supposed inability to disable AI overview and we won!”
She added: “It’s a triumph over Google’s bullying.”
The accessibility of AI on district computers has been a persisting issue after senior administrators imposed a moratorium on its use by students for the current school year. Under that moratorium, students learn about AI but were not to use it in class or on district assignments.
Similarly, New York City schools have put in place a one-year moratorium on student AI through eighth grade. Chancellor Kamar Samuels called Google’s looming search policy, set to take effect early next year, “an ultimatum” and said the city “will look at other options.”
Google did not respond directly to questions about the block or its interactions with L.A. Unified, but defended its intentions.
“We hear parents and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and we share the same goal: help students learn,” the company said in a statement.
The company has cast AI as a positive for schools if pursued in partnership with the corporation, using carefully crafted tools.
“We believe AI products should support ‘productive struggle’ — enabling students to be actively challenged without getting so overwhelmed that they give up,” Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president and general manager for education, wrote in a Nov. 3 post.
He spoke of the company’s Guided Learning platform “as an interactive study tool that coaches students through the process of problem solving through open-ended questions and step-by-step breakdowns. Our research shows that Guided Learning leads to measurable learning gains for students, and we’re now bringing Guided Learning to more products.”
As an example Phillips cited a student pasting a complex physics problem into Google.
“They’ll see prompts to help them think critically and work through the concepts, without going directly to the answer,” Phillips wrote. “We’re starting with a pilot in select U.S. schools later this month to gather and incorporate educator feedback before expanding to other school districts in the coming months.”
Not yet impressed is Associate Professor Stephen J. Aguilar of the USC Rossier School of Education, who said Google’s new move “is reckless.”
“Searching for something became ‘googling it,’ because Google offered a valuable service,” Aguilar said. “They did so not out of the goodness of their hearts — they knew that the ubiquity of their search engine would allow them to capture ad revenue since they control how people most find information,” he said.
“There is no evidence that AI-enabled search is better, and in many instances, there is evidence that it can undermine the necessary friction needed to teach digital literacy and critical thinking,” Aguilar said.
A student’s “productive struggle,” or learning, is at the heart of criticisms.
“There’s too much evidence by now of cognitive offloading and eroded performance, as opposed to building of students’ skills,” said Heather Schwartz, RAND’s director of education, employment and infrastructure, in a presentation to L.A. Unified board members. “High-quality research is showing that there’s harm when AI replaces a student’s first attempt at the work.”
School board member Kelly Gonez, like other critics, focused on the timing of Google’s recent announcement that AI would be inseparable from Google’s search function.
“My personal read on this was [of] a very cynical effort to really hold school districts hostage, and the timing is not coincidental, right?” Gonez said at the November meeting of board Ad Hoc AI committee. “The nation’s two largest school districts take a strong strong stand to protect our students from AI, and then one of the largest tech companies says, ‘Well, no, you have to.’”
Google’s aim in the education space is to build brand loyalty, said Assistant Professor Fanna Gamal at UCLA School of Law. But “acclimating students to Google is increasingly synonymous with acclimating students to AI.”
“School districts like Los Angeles have made it clear that they do not wish to accustom students to AI when its educational value is still in question and when the technology is unpopular with many parents and educators,” said Gamal, whose areas of specialty include education and technology.
The disclosure about the block came after Lee and fellow parent Anya Meksin were guest presenters at the AI committee meeting of Nov. 13. At that meeting, the parents brought forward evidence that some students still were able to use some applications that were supposed to be blocked. This was in addition to the ongoing inability to block Google’s AI overview, parents said.
District staff did not contest that their blocking efforts were a work in progress.
But within a day or two after the meeting, the block was achieved — progress that was unearthed by the Schools Beyond Screens group and later verified by L.A. Unified.
The district still has no direct control over students’ use of AI on their own devices.
School board member Nick Melvoin, who has generally advocated for more district openness in its operations and in providing records, said he could understand why district staff might be inclined to be cagey or obtuse in disclosing what they accomplished.
“The more that we share what’s possible” in terms of a block, “maybe Google will find a workaround,” Melvoin said in an interview. “Will they create a version that can’t be blocked?”
