articles.title_orig: Earliest iron scale armor in China found near First Emperor’s tomb
articles.title_zh: Earliest iron scale armor in China found near First Emperor’s tomb
articles.content_orig:
Archaeologists working beside the mausoleum of China’s First Emperor have uncovered what appears to be the earliest complete suit of iron scale armor ever found in the country. A team from University College London and the Emperor Qin Shihuang’s Mausoleum Site Museum reported the find in the journal Antiquity.
The armor came from tomb M1, the third of nine large tombs stretching west of the emperor’s main burial enclosure. Crews excavated the site from 2013 to 2023. The main chamber covers 1,900 square meters and sits 15.6 meters below ground. Inside, the team found two coffins, a four-wheeled wooden carriage and horse-and-chariot burials in side pits. No other Qin tomb dug so far is richer or better preserved. Nobody knows who lay there, but the person held high rank.
The iron scales sat in a heap on the south side of the chamber. The ceiling collapsed long ago, and the scales likely dropped from a shelf. Corrosion broke most of the metal into tiny pieces, yet the team still counted at least 200 larger fragments. They estimate the suit held 800 to 1,200 scales. A helmet would need only 80 to 90, and several suits would need far more, so the pile points to one body piece. Such a garment would weigh about 10 kilograms.
Most scales are small rectangles, roughly 33 by 29 millimeters and 1.5 millimeters thick, with 10 tiny holes for lacing. A heavier type has 11 holes, and a few fish-scale shapes turned up too. Mapping with micro X-ray fluorescence found traces of cinnabar, a red mercury pigment, on nearly every scale tested. Some pieces carry flakes of a black coating, likely lacquer. The team found no gold or silver plating. A Han Dynasty iron suit from Linzi, which held 2,142 scales, was gilded.
Under a scanning electron microscope, five scales showed low-carbon steel, with 0.1 to 0.4 percent carbon. Grains measured 10 to 20 microns across, a sign of heavy hammering. Slag was scarce. Smiths most likely started with cast iron, stripped out carbon in a process called fining, and forged the result into thin sheets. This matches what researchers know about Qin iron work. The small sample leaves room for another route, direct smelting of solid iron.
The mausoleum holds other armor made of different materials. The Terracotta Army wears clay armor, and the brown scales seem to copy leather. Smaller gray scales on some higher-ranking figures might stand in for iron. In pit K9801, crews dug only about 1 percent of the area and pulled out 87 stone corselets and 43 stone helmets. Their scales look much like the M1 scales and were laced with flat copper wire.
Qin law texts written on bamboo slips hint at the cost. A penalty of making one set of scale armor equaled 168 to 224 days of labor. The authors say an iron suit, with smaller scales and finer lacing, might have kept a small workshop busy for a year or more.
One puzzle remains. Iron swords also lay in tomb M1, yet the mausoleum holds tens of thousands of bronze weapons. Some scholars think the bronze was symbolic. Old reign dates on weapons from Pit 1 suggest the army drew on aging stock. The authors don’t settle the debate. They plan to study more iron tools and weapons from the complex.

articles.title_orig: ‘Mass-casualty event’ in Europe possible amid rise in Russian sabotage, says thinktank
articles.title_zh: ‘Mass-casualty event’ in Europe possible amid rise in Russian sabotage, says thinktank
articles.content_orig:
Alleged Russia-directed sabotage in Europe is intensifying, with the possibility of a mass-casualty event as Moscow reportedly targets infrastructure like rail lines, airports and energy networks, a new report from a prominent international think tank warns.
While it is not directly at war with any European nation other than Ukraine, Moscow is engaged in a conflict via proxies intended to weaken the continent’s support for Kyiv, the report says.
Russia has increasingly turned to sabotage over the past year, with the use of explosives and arson roughly doubling and presenting a risk of mass casualties, the report from the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), released Thursday, says.
Such a disaster could bring calls for retaliation and possibly divide European governments, it says.
Germany and Poland, the European countries whose logistics and industries play the largest roles in support of Ukraine, are seeing the greater percentage of reported Russian sabotage, with more than half of incidents recorded between October 2025 and September of this year in those countries, according to the report’s findings.
According to an analysis by the IISS, 29 Moscow-linked incidents were recorded between October 2025 and September 2026 in Poland, including a November 2025 incident in which an explosive charge damaged a rail line linking Warsaw to the Ukraine border. Though there were no casualties, Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said later the explosion was likely planned to destroy a train.
“Attacks have focused on sectors critical to the Ukrainian war effort, while attacks on public infrastructure and high-profile locations also appear to be intended to undermine public confidence and support for Ukraine,” the report says.
Before the report’s release, US President Donald Trump’s top envoy for Russia-Ukraine negotiations and son-in-law Jared Kushner, praised Russian leader Vladimir Putin’s “restraint” in the more than four-year-old war.
“He’s agreed not to use nuclear weapons, which obviously is a big thing,” Kushner told Mathias Döpfner, CEO of POLITICO’s parent company Axel Springer, in a podcast that debuted Wednesday.
But the IISS report says it’s so-called “unconventional war” – not nuclear war – that poses an immediate threat to Europe.
One every four minutes: 720,000 Russian soldiers killed since start of Ukraine war, new data suggests
Russian intelligence services have been able to recruit a force of proxies who are likely becoming better at sabotage, using “more complex methods, including improvised explosive devices armed with timers and detonators,” the report says.
Despite the arrests of proxies in several instances – along with the expulsion of Russian intelligence officers and closure of some consulates – the Europeans have not deterred Moscow, it says.
“There is no clear evidence that these measures have made sabotage a less attractive instrument of Kremlin policy,” it says.
A pool of proxy recruits does not seem to be deterred either, it says, as the frequency of attacks has not changed substantially.
“Arrests impose costs on proxies, but so far not on the (Russian intelligence services) that direct and enable them,” the report says.
The report also says Russian-backed sabotage comes in surges across the continent, suggesting central planning in Moscow.
But it also notes that there is evidence of one proxy network coordinating attacks in several countries, and that there may be competing networks so that disrupting one may not deter another.
Overall, Russia’s actions are being conducted on tactical and strategic levels, according to the report, with tactical operations trying to damage or delay aid for Ukraine, while strategically trying to make support for Kyiv too economically or politically costly for European governments to bear.
Meanwhile, Kushner pointed a finger at Europe for the prolonged length of the war in Ukraine, saying “provocative” statements and actions coming out of European capitals have put Putin on guard.
“His view is he does not see that (the Europeans) are ready for peace. He thinks they want the strategic defeat of Russia,” Kushner told the podcast “MD Meets,” which went online Wednesday .
But Kushner said Washington has put no pressure on Ukraine, despite cutting military and logistical aid during the conflict.
He told the POLITICO podcast the country’s “courage and bravery and capability is one of the greatest stories we’ve seen in many, many decades.”
But he was more circumspect of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who he said has wrongly “attacked” Trump.
“You would think that President Zelensky would be trying to engage with (Trump) respectfully,” Kushner said.

The military alleged the commercial vessel had "precision munitions."
Talks between the U.S. and Iran remain stalled despite the two countries signing a memorandum of understanding in June, aimed at ending the war that began with joint American-Israeli strikes on the country in February. The opening strikes killed a host of top Iranian officials and commanders, among them Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
The two sides have continued to exchange strikes, though have not returned to the intense fighting seen in the early stages of the conflict. The U.S. says it is enforcing a naval blockade of the country's Persian Gulf and Gulf of Oman ports, while Iran claims control over the strategic Strait of Hormuz and continues to claim attacks on shipping transiting the waterway.
Meanwhile, intensified fighting between Saudi-backed Yemeni forces and Iran-backed Houthi rebels in Yemen has seen the latter repeatedly attack Saudi military, oil infrastructure and transport facilities.
See the most recent developments below.
U.S. Central Command said it disabled a commercial vessel with "precision munitions" in the Gulf of Oman Thursday after the ship allegedly tried to run the U.S. Naval blockade against Iran.
The U.S. military struck the ship's stern, disabling propulsion of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer shortly after it left an Iranian port, according to CENTCOM.
The military said that the ship's civilian crew was unharmed.
Gen. Sardar Shekarchi, spokesperson of Iran's armed forces, denies that Iran carried out a drone attack on Kuwait.
According to Iran's official state news agency IRNA, Shekarchi "categorically and completely" rejected claims by the Kuwaiti military that Iranian forces attacked vital Kuwaiti sites.
"No military or offensive operations have been conducted by the Armed Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran in the region," Shekarchi said, according to IRNA.
"Given the history of hostile actions -- including the use of 'false flag' tactics and regional adventurism by the Zionist regime and U.S. forces -- these accusations should be viewed as a cover for continued malevolence and an attempt to exacerbate insecurity in the region," Shekarchi said.
Kuwaiti authorities have blamed Iran for the attack that killed two Italian nationals and injured one Kuwaiti and one Pakistani national.
-ABC News' Jamie Dorrington
The two Italian nationals injured in Thursday's Iranian drone attack in Kuwait have died, a spokesperson for Kuwait's Ministry of Defense said in a statement.
Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni expressed her condolences to the victim's families in a post on X.
"On behalf of myself and the Government, I express my deepest sorrow and extend my heartfelt condolences to the victims' families. My thoughts are with all those affected by the attack and their families," Meloni said.
The Kuwait Army on Thursday reported that four people were injured by falling shrapnel after an Iranian drone attack targeted "a vital site" in the Gulf state.
The army said in a post to X that Kuwaiti forces "dealt with" the incoming drones. "Material damage also occurred," the statement added.
Those injured were two Italian nationals, one Pakistani national and one Kuwaiti national, the army said.

articles.title_orig: Europe Bets Big On CV90 Armored Fighting Vehicle
articles.title_zh: Europe Bets Big On CV90 Armored Fighting Vehicle
articles.content_orig:
Five European NATO members have signed a landmark agreement to jointly procure more than 400 CV90 series infantry fighting vehicles, in a deal valued at approximately $6 billion. The agreement is one of the biggest multinational land systems procurements in recent European history and could offer a model for rebuilding the continent’s armored forces, as NATO seeks to strengthen its posture in the face of the growing threat from Russia .
The contracts were signed today at the Swedish Army Museum in Stockholm, with Sweden, Finland, Norway, Lithuania, and the Netherlands participating. The vehicles will be produced by BAE Systems Hägglunds and share a common CV9035 MkIV Nordic Edition configuration, although individual countries will retain differences in terms of equipment, including communications, electronic warfare, and battle management systems.
The significance of the agreement lies not just in the number of vehicles involved. European countries have traditionally procured major land systems through separate national programs, often resulting in different configurations and multiple supply chains, not to mention duplicated development and support costs. The CV90 agreement represents a major effort to overcome those inefficiencies by bringing a group of countries together around a common vehicle configuration, coordinated production, and more closely aligned support arrangements.
In doing so, it provides a tangible example of the kind of multinational defense industrial cooperation European governments have increasingly called for as they seek to rebuild military capabilities following Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, while at the same time because U.S. security guarantees are now not necessarily taken for granted.
“This joint procurement of the CV90 strengthens NATO’s capabilities and creates opportunities for both effective and close cooperation around the system between our five countries,” Swedish Minister of Defense Pål Jonson said.
Together with 🇳🇴 🇫🇮 🇱🇹 🇳🇱, Sweden has signed a joint procurement of CV90 infantry fighting vehicles. This strengthens NATO's warfighting capability, enhances security of supply in Europe, and proves the quality of Swedish defence industry. 🇸🇪🛡️ pic.twitter.com/v7MZ3LnmIy
There is a long history of European efforts to achieve greater commonality in armored vehicle procurement, and an equally long record of falling short. During the Cold War, attempts to develop a common European tank repeatedly foundered on competing national requirements and disagreements over industrial responsibilities. A Franco-German effort in the late 1950s produced separate national outcomes — the Leopard 1 and AMX-30 — while later Franco-German and Anglo-German projects also failed to deliver a shared tank. Even the ambitious U.S.-German MBT-70 program, intended to replace both countries’ existing tanks with a common design, collapsed amid spiraling costs and incompatible requirements.
NATO did achieve some useful standardization, notably around ammunition and other elements of logistics, but it never translated that into a common fleet of armored vehicles. The result was a collection of national designs, often built around different operational priorities and industrial bases. The CV90 initiative takes a more pragmatic route. Instead of trying to design an entirely new vehicle to satisfy every participant, it brings several countries together around an existing, mature platform and a shared configuration, for a more achievable starting point.
Originally developed in Sweden starting in the mid-1980s, the CV90 already has a substantial NATO footprint. It is in service with Denmark, Estonia, Finland, the Netherlands, Norway and Sweden, while the Czech Republic and Slovakia have also ordered the type. Switzerland, although not a NATO member, is another established operator, and Ukraine has joined the CV90 user community . BAE Systems lists 10 nations operating or contracted to receive the vehicle, across 17 variants. That gives the Nordic initiative a significant base of existing users with which to share experience, support arrangements, and future upgrades. However, the different national configurations mean that there will be limitations on commonality.
Sweden will acquire 60 CV90 MkIVs under the agreement. Finland is purchasing 160 vehicles in a deal valued at approximately $2.15 billion, including maintenance kits, testing equipment, technical documentation, training, and licenses. Lithuania had previously announced plans to acquire 100 vehicles as part of the multinational program. The remaining quantities for Norway and the Netherlands have not been publicly detailed, although the combined initial order exceeds 400 vehicles.
Maavoimille hankitaan 160 uutta CV9035NE-taisteluajoneuvoa. Hankinnalla kehitetään  jalkaväen liikkuvuutta, tulivoimaa ja kykyä toimia läpinäkyvällä taistelukentällä. https://t.co/CNuqkmMvar pic.twitter.com/v0bMLBmyO7
The Finnish acquisition is particularly significant as Helsinki looks to replace its aging Soviet-era BMP-2 infantry fighting vehicles, which are increasingly difficult to support. The new CV90s are expected to begin entering Finnish service from around 2030, while BAE Systems Hägglunds has indicated that deliveries across the broader program could begin as early as 2029.
The CV9035 MkIV represents the latest major evolution of the CV90 family, which has developed through successive generations since entering service in the early 1990s. BAE Systems describes it as a fifth-generation iteration of the combat-proven platform, incorporating significant improvements in mobility, payload capacity, electronic architecture, and crew capabilities.
One of the most important changes is the introduction of a Scania diesel engine producing up to 1,000 horsepower, coupled with an upgraded Allison heavy-duty transmission. The drivetrain improvements are intended to provide greater mobility and acceleration while accommodating the additional weight associated with modern protection systems, sensors, and mission equipment.
The MkIV also introduces active damping technology, designed to improve suspension performance, vehicle handling, and stability over difficult terrain. Its gross vehicle weight rating increases from 35 to 37 tonnes, providing a useful boost in payload capacity. This gives operators greater flexibility to accommodate future protection enhancements, sensors, electronic warfare systems, and other mission equipment.
The vehicle also incorporates a NATO-standard electronic architecture and BAE Systems’ iFighting concept , intended to improve crew situational awareness and decision-making through enhanced ergonomics, digital integration, augmented reality, and autonomous support technologies.
Its armament includes a 35mm cannon, co-axial machine gun, and anti-tank guided missiles , providing a combination of direct-fire support and the ability to engage armored targets at longer ranges.
The war in Ukraine has raised serious questions about the survivability and utility of armored vehicles on a modern battlefield in the face of persistent drone threats, in terms of both surveillance and kinetic attack . Nevertheless, the conflict has not rendered armor obsolete. Rather, it has highlighted the challenges of employing armored forces in an increasingly contested battlespace. The continued investment in armored capabilities by major militaries around the world demonstrates that they still regard armored vehicles as an important component of modern land warfare, even as their roles, protection requirements, and methods of employment evolve.
The CV90 has already seen combat use in Ukraine, where Swedish-donated vehicles have been employed by Ukrainian forces . Of the more than 125 CV90s given to Ukraine, at least 25 have been destroyed, damaged, or captured according to the Oryx open-source tracking group . articles.title_orig: Stocks snap from a $6 trillion washout to a $3.5 trillion surge as Nvidia, Micron, and SpaceX bounce back
articles.title_zh: Stocks snap from a $6 trillion washout to a $3.5 trillion surge as Nvidia, Micron, and SpaceX bounce back
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Wall Street is no longer running for the exits as chipmakers pull stocks off Wednesday's lows. Main Street is still headed the other way.
The S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) fell almost 9% last week , its worst week since April 2025, and lost nearly $6 trillion in market value. On Monday alone, it gained about $3 trillion , putting in its best day since April 2025.
On Wednesday morning, the S&P 500 fell more than 3%, and the Nasdaq-100 ( ^NDX ) briefly sat 20% below its record close, the line for a bear market . That came as a hot inflation report and new tariff proposals hit. By the close, both were down less than 1%.
Friday's half-day session gave the S&P 500 its best Thanksgiving week since 2008 and its best week since April 2025, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. The index rose almost 6% for the week, while the Nasdaq 100 gained almost 7%.
Monday's surge came as Nvidia's ( NVDA ) board brought back Jensen Huang at the White House's urging. "The Trump put was exercised on Monday," Interactive Brokers chief strategist Steve Sosnick told Yahoo Finance on Wednesday. "Trump put" is Wall Street's shorthand for a president who steps in when stocks fall, much like a put option protects against losses.
Chips have done the heavy lifting. Nvidia finished the week up about 20%, adding roughly $600 billion in market value. Micron ( MU ), SK Hynix ( SKHY ), AMD ( AMD ), and SanDisk ( SNDK ) closed roughly 15% to 27% above their Wednesday lows. SpaceX ( SPCX ) and Tesla ( TSLA ) rose about 5% Friday , and Anthropic ( ANT ) jumped about 11%, climbing back above its $83 IPO price.
Everyday investors weren't the ones rushing back in. Leaving out Nvidia and Anthropic, retail traders sold a net of almost $350 million of single stocks on Monday, according to Vanda Research. It was their biggest one-day sale since March 2020, even as the Nasdaq-100 jumped almost 7%.
"The 2026 retail investor is very much a different beast, and one that is unwilling to be a buyer of last resort in an equity drawdown," Vanda's Viraj Patel wrote Wednesday.
The S&P 500 has bounced back this hard after an 8% weekly drop only seven other times since 1950. Two of the last three, in March 2020 and April 2025, marked the bottom. The other five came before more losses.
If Monday's jump can hold, history says the odds of the rally continuing improve.
Since 1993, the SPDR S&P 500 ETF ( SPY ) has opened a Monday 2% or more higher 20 times. The five times it gave back at least half that gain by Wednesday, it broke the prior Friday's low within three months. This time, SPY gave back less than a fifth of Monday's gain by Wednesday's close. When that happened before, SPY stayed above the prior Friday's low two out of three times.
Asked whether the rebound is a dead-cat bounce , a brief recovery in a falling market, Sosnick wasn't ready to call it.
"It's too early to say," he said. "There wasn't really a fundamental policy shift."

articles.title_orig: China is making inroads into Europe’s skies with cheap plane fuel. Brussels takes aim
articles.title_zh: China is making inroads into Europe’s skies with cheap plane fuel. Brussels takes aim
articles.content_orig:
Not all green fuel comes with a green light / Photo: Pexels
Cheap green fuel from abroad could help Europe clean up its skies, but it may also ground the continent’s own producers. Brussels is now launching an anti-dumping investigation into imports from China and Singapore, amid claims that low-priced Asian competition is squeezing European manufacturers out of the market.
The EU wants more sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) in its aircraft tanks. But cheap imports from Asia could undermine the European industry it hopes to build.
The European Commission has therefore launched an anti-dumping investigation into SAF imports from China and Singapore. The probe will examine not only the price of the finished fuel, but also the conditions under which Chinese producers obtain a key raw material.
The European Biodiesel Board (EBB) filed the complaint on 15 October on behalf of European sustainable aviation fuel producers. It argues that imports from both Asian countries are growing and capturing an increasing share of the EU market.
Their rising volumes and low prices are putting pressure on European producers’ sales. According to the complaint, this is taking a toll on their overall performance and financial health.
In a notice published in the Official Journal, the Commission said the evidence submitted was sufficient to justify opening an investigation. This does not yet mean dumping has been established. The investigation must determine whether it is actually taking place.
One particularly interesting aspect of the complaint concerns China’s market for raw materials. SAF producers use, among other things, used cooking oil (UCO). According to the document, it accounts for around 70 per cent of the fuel’s production costs.
The EBB claims that UCO prices in China are significantly lower than those on comparable international markets.
The government also intervenes in how the raw material is exported. “According to the evidence in the complaint, used cooking oil (…) is not subject to VAT rebate on exports from the People’s Republic of China,” the Commission’s notice states.
This keeps a key feedstock on the domestic market, allowing China to focus on producing and exporting a higher-value product. The Commission will examine whether these conditions distort feedstock prices and give Chinese producers an unfair competitive advantage.
The investigation into China will also look at wider state intervention in the economy. The complaint points to the influence of China’s financial system, land market and labour conditions on fuel production and sales.
It argues that domestic prices and costs cannot provide a reliable basis for comparison. Instead, it proposes using Thailand as a reference country when calculating the product’s normal value.
The approach to Singapore is different. The Commission lacks reliable data on domestic prices there. It will therefore calculate normal value using production costs, administrative and selling expenses, and profit.
Sustainable aviation fuel is one way to reduce aviation’s carbon footprint . Unlike conventional kerosene, it comes from renewable feedstocks or waste streams. It can also be used without completely overhauling existing aircraft or aviation infrastructure.
That makes SAF a key part of the EU’s plans to green air transport. The ReFuelEU Aviation Regulation gradually raises the minimum share of sustainable fuels that aviation fuel suppliers must provide at EU airports.
The requirement started at two per cent in 2025. It will rise to six per cent in 2030 and 70 per cent by 2050.
As mandatory demand grows, new producers and investment in European production capacity have an opportunity to emerge. But competing against fuel made at significantly lower costs could make life harder for European companies.
This creates an awkward contradiction. Cheaper imports can help meet rising demand for low-carbon fuel. At the same time, they could weaken the domestic industry expected to sustain the transition in the long run.
The anti-dumping investigation will establish whether SAF enters the EU at prices below its normal value. It will also assess whether this causes injury to European producers.
If the allegations are confirmed, the Commission could impose additional duties on imports from the countries concerned. But this is not automatic. It must establish dumping, injury to the European industry and a causal link between the two.
The Commission also plans to register imports of SAF from China and Singapore from the early stages of the investigation. This matters for importers, too. “This may lead to retroactive collection of definitive duties on registered imports,” the Commission warns.
The investigation must conclude within 14 months of the notice’s publication. The Commission could introduce provisional duties after around seven to eight months.

articles.title_zh: Stock Market News Nov. 27, 2026: Dow zooms higher, clinches best week since 2022 as stocks rebound in holiday-shortened trade
articles.content_orig:
U.S. equities rose on Friday as investors wrapped up a turbulent, holiday-shortened trading week.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average was higher by 591.99 points, or 1.18%, to close at 50,774.94. The S&P 500 added 1.6% to end the day at 7,297.49, while the Nasdaq Composite advanced 2.31% to 24,129.50. The moves come amid a volatile week during an even more volatile month.
Technology stocks supported Friday's bounce. "Magnificent Seven" members Meta Platforms and Amazon popped more than 3% and about 4%, respectively, while chipmaker Broadcom increased almost 4%. Shares of artificial intelligence lab Anthropic added nearly 11%.
The major U.S. stock benchmarks posted strong weekly gains. The Dow and S&P 500 were both up more than 5%. The former notched its biggest weekly advance since October 2022, while the latter posted its best week since April 2025. The Nasdaq has surged more than 6%, scoring its largest weekly gain since April.
The week kicked off with Jensen Huang getting reinstated as CEO at Nvidia , a move that sent the stock up 31% during Monday's session and drove the S&P 500 and Nasdaq to post their best days since April 2025 . The Dow advanced more than 1,400 points, or roughly 3%.
Since then, however, the S&P 500 and Nasdaq have come under pressure as Nvidia and other AI-related stocks have given back some of Monday's gains.
Prior to Huang's departure earlier this month, sentiment toward the AI trade was already downbeat, with investors growing concerned about debt financing , signs of moderation in capital expenditures and Democratic wins in the midterm elections resulting in a slowdown in data center development .
But Ben Fulton of WEBs Investments believes the fears surrounding AI, except for those regarding debt financing, are "a bit overblown," noting that the "biggest risk" is whether AI companies can "keep funding the growth they need." At the same time, he doesn't think investors can "afford to be out of the AI story."
"The risk seems to be on the upside right now," the CEO said. "You don't want to be short this market, at least the AI names."
To be sure, others believe that while there are long-term anxieties with the AI trade, the recent weakness in the market has had more to do with the prospect of the Federal Reserve raising interest rates . The latest personal consumption expenditures price index reading this week reinforced traders' expectations for multiple hikes over the coming months.
The U.S. stock market was closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving, and closed on Friday at 1 p.m. ET.
The three leading U.S. indexes ended Friday's session solidly higher.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average added 591.99 points, or 1.18%, to close at 50,774.94. The S&P 500 ended up 1.6% at 7,297.49, while the Nasdaq Composite gained 2.31% to settle at 24,129.50.
Brent crude oil prices are on track for weekly gains as Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen continue to target Saudi Arabia's energy infrastructure.
Brent crude, the international benchmark, has gained nearly 2% this week, while U.S. West Texas Intermediate has fallen more than 1%. Brent was last down more than 2% to trade just above $94 a barrel during Friday's session. U.S. crude oil fell 1% to trade above $82 a barrel.
The Saudi Energy Ministry said its Jazan refinery was attacked, killing at least one worker and leaving several others injured. The Houthis claimed on Wednesday that they had struck the kingdom's energy hub at Ras Tanura.
Gold and silver prices are rising after trending sharply lower this month.
Gold futures were up 2.6% at $3,628.00 an ounce. Silver futures rose 7.9% to $43.23 an ounce. The contracts are down almost 7% and more than 12%, respectively, in November.
Stock markets have been skittish in November.
Just look at the VIX volatility index , a gauge of how much the S&P 500 might move in the next 30 days based on options trading, which pulled back to 25.13 on Friday.
The VIX, a gauge of skittishness on Wall Street, has tumbled about 30% so far this week, one week after soaring 86% to close at 35.89 last Friday Nov. 20.
The week before that, the VIX tumbled almost 25% to close at 19.3 on Nov. 13. In the week ended Nov. 6, the VIX soared 32% to end at 25.64.
Shares for Anthropic jumped over 8% on Friday during a broader tech rally following a selloff earlier this week. The AI company went public last Thursday.
Investors have flocked to retailers like Walmart and Costco Wholesale while souring on AI names like Nvidia and SpaceX . The trade makes sense amid worries that AI capex growth has peaked and the next wave will be consolidation.
Analysts may just be starting to cut estimates on AI names, making aggregate forecasts a bit stale.
Debt financing has dried up and data centers builders will need more guarantees on leases. Nvidia has been at the center of AI financing. But the outlook is murkier as CEO Jensen Huang faces Congressional hearings and investigations into the company's sales practices in Asia.
SpaceX has become an AI battleground too, as CEO Elon Musk ramps up capex for data centers and rocket launches, among other ventures.
The retailers, conversely, are looking safer as consumer spending stays strong and Americans try to stretch their budgets amid elevated inflation and fuel prices. With affordability top of mind, Walmart and Costco have a natural edge.
But the retailers' stocks are no deals, while those in the AI zone trade at bargain prices, even assuming some haircuts to earnings estimates.
Valuation multiples – rather than core earnings – have been compressing due to higher interest rates, and that means that higher cash flow companies could be good bets in the market now, according to Sarat Sethi, Managing Partner and Portfolio Manager/Equity Analyst at Douglas C. Lane & Associates.
For this reason, Sethi likes the industrials sector and airplane-maker Boeing in particular.
"I think [there are] opportunities across the market. It doesn't necessarily have to be in tech," he told CNBC on Friday. "For companies like a Boeing that are down 25% … investors are selling it going into year-end, and we think these are opportunities to buy high-quality cash flow companies."
The three major averages began Friday's session with gains.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average rose 507 points, or 1%, just after the opening bell. The S&P 500 gained 1.2%, while the Nasdaq Composite jumped 1.5%.
Check out CNBC's live blog here for more on the stocks making moves before the bell.
Analysts with Evercore ISI are on the lookout for a potential frontier AI algorithm from Amazon that could rival top-of-the-line products from Anthropic and OpenAI. They think it could be announced at the company's re:Invent conference in Las Vegas next week.
"Recall that in Q2, [management] said it is pursuing its own frontier model and expected at least a half dozen comparably capable models within a few years, adding that 'one of them will be ours,'" Mark Mahaney at Evercore ISI wrote in a Nov. 25 note to clients.
Evercore is also watching for developments on Bedrock, which is Amazon's interface, or API, for using and coordinating frontier models from other companies. Progress on Amazon's Trainium4 chips and on general AI profitability and agent monetization are also key points of interest.
Nvidia Blackwell chips, barred from being shipped to China, were installed at a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang, according to Bloomberg , adding to scrutiny of the chipmaker's ties to the Chinese firm, Megaspeed, which Alice Huang founded.
Megaspeed has faced scrutiny over concerns that advanced Nvidia chips were diverted to China. Shares of Nvidia are up nearly 2.5%.
European stock markets were broadly higher on Friday morning, as investors continued to pile back into equities after a sell-off across Tuesday and Wednesday fueled by technology and tariff jitters.

articles.title_orig: Putin Visits Russia’s New Nuclear Submarine as Kremlin Says Russia Is “Surrounded by Enemies”
articles.title_zh: Putin Visits Russia’s New Nuclear Submarine as Kremlin Says Russia Is “Surrounded by Enemies”
articles.content_orig:
Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov claimed that Russia is surrounded by enemies and stated that the country’s security relies on its nuclear triad.
According to Peskov, this strategic deterrent includes land-based intercontinental ballistic missiles, nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarines, and strategic bombers, as reported by The Moscow Times on November 27.
We bring you stories from the ground. Your support keeps our team in the field.
He noted that Russia’s nuclear forces prove their necessity every day in the current geopolitical environment.
“Our country currently exists in a very, very hostile environment, so the nuclear triad is a reliable guarantee of our security,” Peskov said.
Peskov made these remarks while commenting on Vladimir Putin’s Friday visit to Severodvinsk, where the Russian leader attended a flag-raising ceremony for the nuclear-powered submarine cruiser Perm, The Moscow Times reported.
Putin was also scheduled to hold a meeting on the development of the Russian Navy’s nuclear submarines during the trip.
Putin called for upgrading submarine weaponry so the fleet can carry out combat missions in any part of the world’s oceans, Russian outlet Agentstvo reported. He stated that all branches of the Navy must possess significant strike power to counter enemy naval groups and hit strategic targets, adding that the strategy and tactics of naval warfare are changing.
“Therefore, alongside the construction of new submarines of various types, it is important to improve their weaponry and, above all, systematically enhance the tactical and technical characteristics of long-range high-precision weapons and anti-ship missiles,” Putin said. “This will make it possible to build up the strike capabilities of naval groups to carry out combat missions in any area of the world’s oceans.”
Putin also noted the need to involve high-tech medium and small businesses in this cooperation, while the newly commissioned nuclear-powered submarine Perm is set to reinforce Russia’s Pacific Fleet.
Agentstvo noted that Putin’s remarks come amid an expanding geography of strikes on Russian vessels during Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine. On November 21, the dry cargo ship Sparta II was attacked in the Gulf of Finland, followed by strikes on two Russian vessels—including the corvette Merkury—off the coast of Libya on November 22.
These statements follow a series of nuclear threats directed at the West by Russian officials. Earlier this week, Deputy Chairman of Russia’s Security Council Dmitry Medvedev stated that Moscow could launch a preemptive nuclear strike if Western countries supply Ukraine with weapons of mass destruction.
Russia previously appeared to have begun deploying its RS-28 Sarmat intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs), despite years of development delays and repeated test failures.
These missiles were designed to carry multiple nuclear warheads and potentially strike the United States from an unconventional southern trajectory.
According to a November 2026 analysis by the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS), satellite imagery suggested that the missiles were entering operational service with Russia’s 62nd Missile Division near Uzhur in the Krasnoyarsk region.

articles.title_orig: US Futures Rally as Tech Rebound Gains Momentum: Markets Wrap
articles.title_zh: US Futures Rally as Tech Rebound Gains Momentum: Markets Wrap
articles.content_orig:
SpaceX shares rose 4.83% in Friday's shortened trading session, amid broader Nasdaq gains and after CEO Elon Musk expanded his SpaceX share-donation plan for U.S. children.
Other tech-related stocks, including Micron , Qualcomm , Lumentum and Tesla all gained over 5% on Friday as the sector rebounded from a heavy sell-off earlier this week. SanDisk was Friday's biggest mover as investors rotated back into some AI trade names , surging 15.96%.
Musk posted on X on Thursday, "I will be donating another share of SpaceX to all kids in America every year."
After Musk's post, SpaceX shares jumped more than 7% in overnight trading on Blue Ocean ATS, an alternative trading system for U.S. equities that runs during the nighttime hours. U.S. stock exchanges were closed Thursday for the Thanksgiving holiday and closed at 1 p.m. ET on Friday.
Shares closed 1.30% higher on Wednesday ahead of Thanksgiving.
The latest pledge follows SpaceX's announcement Wednesday that it would donate one share of its Class A stock to all active Trump Accounts, tax-advantaged investment accounts for American children, with Musk personally matching the gift.
In a separate post on X, Musk said SpaceX's contribution would be transferred next month, while his personal donation would follow when his lockup period expires in June next year.
Nearly 70 million Trump Accounts had been created as of October, according to the White House.
Since the program's launch in July, families and friends have contributed more than $1 billion to the accounts, bringing total deposits from all sources to more than $9 billion, CNBC reported earlier this week.
The FCC also announced Wednesday that it granted SpaceX approval to deploy 1 million data center satellites for the company's Starmind constellation.
Speaking on CNBC's "Squawk on the Street" on Friday, FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said the authorization of SpaceX's satellites will have ripple effects within the industry as well.
"Not just SpaceX, but all sorts of different players in this market. Because at the end of the day, we want everyone to compete and succeed. I think we're going to see a lot of players entering this space soon," Carr said.

articles.title_orig: Spanish Police Find a Vast Marijuana Bunker Beneath a Backyard Playground
articles.title_zh: Spanish Police Find a Vast Marijuana Bunker Beneath a Backyard Playground
articles.content_orig:
By Molly Grace •
                                            Published: 26 Nov 2026 • 21:54                                                                • 2 minutes read
Officers lifted the artificial grass and found an access hatch. Photo credit: Guardia Civil/Ministro de Interior
A children’s playground is supposed to be somewhere parents can let their little ones run around without a second thought. But in Granada, the swings, playhouse and artificial grass were hiding something far more sinister: a concealed entrance to an underground cannabis farm containing 1,954 plants.
The underground plantation was found on a property in Las Gabias, where the Guardia Civil uncovered the entrance beneath what appeared to be a small children’s playground. The surface had been dressed with artificial grass, a swing, a playhouse and a small mat. White decorative stone covered the surrounding ground, helping disguise the structure. It was not simply a cannabis farm hidden in a basement. The play area itself concealed a hydraulic hatch and a vehicle ramp leading down into the bunker.
Officers lifted the artificial grass and found an access hatch used to operate a large hydraulic door. Once it was opened, a ramp led down into the underground installation, which measured around 180 square metres and stood five metres high. Inside around 2,000 cannabis plants in two large growing rooms. Both were fitted with lighting, ventilation and climate-control systems designed to support intensive cultivation.
The discovery raises an obvious question about the setting: the entrance had been disguised as a place for children to play. The Guardia Civil has not said that children were present or that the area was being used by children, but the equipment was deliberately arranged to make the concealed access look like an ordinary play space.
Investigators also found an electricity tower which was allegedly being used to make an illegal connection to the power network. The load detected was equivalent to the electricity consumption of around 100 homes.
The bunker was described by the Guardia Civil as the largest and most sophisticated underground cannabis-growing installation discovered so far in Granada province.
The discovery formed part of Operation Nazarí-Sabika 04, an investigation into an alleged criminal organisation involved in growing and processing cannabis and supplying specialist equipment to other drug-trafficking groups across Spain. The operation began more than a year ago and entered its main phase on November 17, when officers carried out 13 searches in Granada city and the municipalities of Albolote, Jun, Las Gabias and Maracena.
Five people were arrested and three others are being investigated on suspicion of drug cultivation and production, electricity fraud, illegal possession of a prohibited weapon and membership of a criminal group. The alleged ringleader has been remanded in custody. Across the three plantations uncovered during the searches, officers seized 2,479 cannabis plants. They also confiscated two cars, two vans, a caravan, a trailer, a stun gun and €22,970 in cash.
Officers also sealed premises specialising in cannabis-growing equipment, known as a grow shop, which was allegedly linked to the organisation. The Guardia Civil estimates its value at several million euros. Investigators believe the shop’s owner used it to obtain equipment for the underground plantation and to supply products to other locations around Spain.
The investigation was carried out by the Guardia Civil’s criminal intelligence and Policía Judicial units in Granada, together with officers from its Las Gabias investigation team.

articles.title_orig: Spain’s Pedro Sanchez bets on left-wing voting surge to defy election polls
articles.title_zh: Spain’s Pedro Sanchez bets on left-wing voting surge to defy election polls
articles.content_orig:
Spain’s Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez appears sure he will secure a left-wing majority in ⁠a snap general election on Sunday, despite adverse public polling suggesting a right-wing advantage.
“I can’t conceive of us losing,” the Socialist leader told radio station SER on Friday, as political parties prepared to wrap up campaigning before the vote.
The outcome of the election will be closely watched as Europe opens an electoral cycle over the next 12 months that could reshape the balance of power within the European Union.
Amid a legal ban on publishing opinion surveys within five days of an election, Sanchez ⁠insisted that internal data suggested his Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party (PSOE) would win the most votes, allowing him to clinch re-election with the support of smaller leftist allies.
He said that left-leaning voters were increasingly mobilising to turn out in droves, a prerequisite for reaching ‌a progressive majority to tackle issues such as the country’s deep housing crisis.
However, nearly all the polls released before the ban showed a clear advantage for a potential coalition between the conservative People’s Party (PP) and far-right Vox, which seek to oust Sanchez after eight years in power.
Earlier, during a televised pre-election debate, Sanchez clashed with PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo and Vox’s Santiago Abascal, as well as Ada Colau, a left-wing Spanish politician and former mayor of Barcelona associated with the Sumar political alliance, in a debate focused on immigration, the housing crisis and foreign policy.
The prime minister criticised the Madrid regional government, controlled by the PP, for awarding an honorary medal to the Israeli government while the assault on Gaza continued.
“It is shameful,” Sanchez said, accusing his opponents of having “no humanity whatsoever.”
He also interrupted Feijoo when the conservative leader described Israel’s actions in Gaza as a “massacre”, insisting that “it is genocide”.
Sanchez warned voters that Spain faced a choice between “regression and progressivism”, arguing that the PP and Vox wanted to replicate the politics of US President Donald Trump and Argentinian President Javier Milei.
Sanchez has vaunted his record on the international stage, notably his outspoken defence of immigration, clashes with Trump and criticism of Israel. The dynamism of the EU’s fourth-largest economy under his leadership has also drawn praise at a turbulent time for global markets.
But a polarising status at home puts his tenure in peril.
Sanchez is holding his final large rally in Madrid on Friday, seeking a late mobilisation of left-wing voters to defeat what he calls the “regression” of a possible PP-Vox coalition.
“We are unstoppable and we will win!” he told a Socialist meeting in the western city of Plasencia, sporting a red T-shirt emblazoned with the slogan “the power of women”.
He contrasted a Spain “of prosperity, principles and values” against a “reactionary coalition” that would question women’s rights, cut pensions and gut public services.
PP leader Feijoo, who won the most seats at the last election in 2023 but failed to form a government, told supporters in Barcelona: “This time we will pull it off.”
Dismissing Sanchez’s campaign of “fear”, he will hold his campaign finale in Seville, capital of the southern Andalusia region.
Addressing reporters before a closing rally in the eastern city of Valencia, Vox leader Abascal accused Sanchez’s “mafia-style” government of “betraying, robbing and lying” to the country.
Spaniards will observe a “day of reflection” on the ‌eve ‌of the vote on Saturday. Campaigning, rallies and political advertising are banned so voters can weigh their choices before heading to the polls.

articles.title_orig: ‘GTA 6’ Is Already One Of The Best-Selling Games Ever, Report Says
articles.title_zh: ‘GTA 6’ Is Already One Of The Best-Selling Games Ever, Report Says
articles.content_orig:
It is technically perfect in its rendition of imperfection, evocative in a way that can’t be explained and must be experienced. And it can be experienced on many different levels.
It is technically perfect in its rendition of imperfection, evocative in a way that can’t be explained and must be experienced. And it can be experienced on many different levels.
Grand Theft Auto VI , the sprawling new video game released last week by Rockstar Games , is the latest edition of the most lucrative media franchise on Earth. How lucrative? It made an estimated $3.8 billion on its first day . That’s bigger than the Avengers. It’s bigger than Harry Potter and the Transphobic Author . It’s bigger than the Super Bowl. It’s the biggest single thing in culture right now. And that appears to be confusing a lot of people who don’t play video games. For the uninitiated, GTA is essentially a sandbox crime simulator. It allows you to steal cars, sell drugs, and run over pedestrians as you flee from the cops you haven’t yet shot. It allows you to stick up a Waffle House, drag an ATM through the streets until it breaks open, and murder every civilian in an only lightly fictionalized rendition of the state of Florida.
The fact that this is the most popular thing on the planet seems to be scrambling many brains. I keep seeing the same question from non-gamers: Why ? Why has this video game broken containment and landed in the center of American and even global public discourse? Why does it make so much money? Why is it everywhere ?
I feel like I am well situated to answer these questions, because, while I’m a normal American dad with a wife and children and a full-time job and all the other indicia of normal adult responsibility, I’m also an avid gamer. Most people who play video games will buy only one or two a year ; I probably buy a new game (often on sale) every six to eight weeks. I generally find at least 10 hours a week to play them—though really, the weeks when I only play 10 hours are, like, “election week” or “a week when a hurricane knocked out my power for days.”
So, with my bona fides out of the way: the first thing I tell non-gamers about GTA , or any video game, is that “it’s art.” Thinking about GTA as art helps to explain everything else that’s happening around it, because GTA is the Mona Lisa of this art form. It is technically perfect in its rendition of imperfection. It is evocative in a way that can’t be explained and must be experienced. And it can be experienced on many different levels. Some people want to see the Mona Lisa just to say that they’ve seen it. Some people will see it and not get what all the fuss is about (the French call those people “Americans”). Some people will see it and feel moved to their core. The same thing happens with GTA : It has a fairly linear “Bonnie and Clyde” type of story with a couple of different endings, but no two people will experience GTA in exactly the same way.
Of course, the Mona Lisa isn’t going to pull out a gun and start shooting paintballs at the other portraits. Nor is she going to remove her top and start shaking her money-maker. So let’s get into that. Yes, GTA is violent and hypersexualized. There is a lot of shooting, there are a lot of boobs and penises, and all the violence and sex is delivered with a steady stream of foul language and crude humor. If you want to be mad at the game, the game will give you something to be mad about, no matter your politics. Indeed, right now the people who are most mad at the game are the white-wing manosphere. The game tracks the relationship between the two main characters (who are in a cis-heteronormative relationship) and essentially encourages you to be a “good boyfriend/girlfriend.” The notion of being nice to a woman has made the manosphere lose its mind. Oh no, the game gives you the option to buy flowers for your girlfriend as part of a quest! Men are doomed! You can also not buy her flowers, or you can, I assume, murder the flower-shop guy and take the flowers (but I didn’t try to do that because I am a normal freaking person whose masculinity is not threatened by showing affection).
Just like the sex—or, in the case of the manosphere, the “acknowledging that a woman is a human being”— the violence in GTA is going to turn a lot of people off. But here’s the thing I think most non-gamers do not understand: GTA isn’t the most violent video game on the market. It’s not in the top 10 violent video games that are broadly popular right now. I wouldn’t even rank GTA VI as the most violent video game I’ve played this year . It’s also not the most sexually explicit game I’ve played recently: Baldur’s Gate 3 (a role-playing game that won Game of the Year in 2023) allows you to play with your characters fully nude, if you want to. It famously lets you have sex with a bear.
GTA is not popular because of the violence or sex. The thing that makes GTA popular is the agency you have over the violence. Yes, you can run over pedestrians, but you can also not do that. You can shoot all the cops in the head as you blast your way out of a bank with cash stuffed in the duffel bag, or you can carefully plan your heist so that you trip no alarms and get away without firing a shot. You can’t play the game as a pacifist (you are a criminal; you will be committing crimes; the authorities will try to stop you from committing crimes; this will often lead to violence), but your ultimate body count is your own and reflects your choices, not the game’s.
It’s that agency that makes GTA a totally different experience from other games that are facially far more violent and bloody. If you put me in an average mission in the popular first-person shooter Call of Duty , I’m going to kill a lot of people. The game will call those people “terrorists” because I’m not supposed to feel bad about killing them, but it will give me no success condition other than murdering every terrorist in the compound. In GTA , by comparison, there was an early mission where my friend was kidnapped by odious redneck pig farmers. They were coded as rednecks so that a certain type of person (namely me) wouldn’t feel bad should violence become necessary. Once I freed him, the game gave me the option of
I went with option 3. GTA is popular not because option 3 exists—option 3 exists in pretty much every video game. GTA is popular because options 1 and 2 also exist , so when you choose option 3 you feel it . It makes the killing more of a personal choice than a gameplay mechanic. Most games allow you to kill; GTA is a success because you don’t have to.
Choice and consequence over murder or mercy is not unique to GTA . In fact, I’ve played a lot of games with far more difficult and engaging murder choices than “kill rednecks, yes/no?” But what makes GTA truly special, and a cultural phenomenon rather than simply a very good video game, is that it is a satirical take on us: America in the 2020s. The game is not set in medieval Europe. There are no dragons or witches. It is set in only lightly fictionalized Florida. If you walk down the street in the GTA ’s main city (called “Vice City”), you will feel like you’re walking around Miami.
The game cost well over a billion dollars and 13 years to make, and part of that budget went toward sending game developers to Miami and around Florida to just watch, observe, and report back. It’s reactive in a way never before seen: Random characters will be having random conversations that don’t involve you, and react as one might expect them to if you pull a gun on them: most will run; some will fight; some will just shrug and be like “joke’s on you, I’m broke.”
You will see every body type, fashion choice, race, color, or creed in the game that you might see on any street in America. You’ll hear music blaring out of certain stores. You’ll see car accidents that don’t involve the player at all. One random character tried to steal my car (it didn’t work out well for him).

Brent rebounded to $96 as Houthi attacks and tightening physical supplies raise the prospect of $100 oil despite oversupply forecasts.
Oil prices are set to post a slight weekly gain, ending a three-week cold streak, with ICE Brent moving up to $96 per barrel on the back of recurring Houthi strikes on key Saudi energy infrastructure, such as the Jizan and Ras Tanura refineries. Defying claims of an impending oversupply, the physical side of oil markets seems to be insinuating shortages again, with Dated Brent nearing $100 per barrel amidst faltering Norwegian supply and lower-than-assumed Iraqi outflows. Next week, once the market restarts in earnest after a Thanksgiving-induced slump in trading, triple digits could be on the table again.
Washington Tests OPEC’s Exit Door. According to Reuters, the Trump administration urged OPEC’s founding members Iraq and Venezuela to consider quitting the oil group and blocked Caracas from paying its membership dues, but Saudi intervention cooled the US pressure campaign on Venezuela.
Baghdad Wants a Bigger Measuring Stick. Iraq rejected a production capacity estimate from DeGolyer and MacNaughton, part of OPEC+’s recalibration of quotas, putting Baghdad’s capacity slightly below 5 million b/d, with Iraq insisting it can pump 5.2 million b/d as OPEC+ is expected to meet this Sunday.
OPEC+ Eyes Quota Freeze Amidst Internal Rows. OPEC+ members reached an in-principle agreement to leave their collective 31.01 million b/d production target unchanged for the first quarter of 2027, preferring to focus on controversial capacity discussions rather than focus on irrelevant output quotas.
Australia Keeps More Gas at Home. Australia’s parliament passed its long-mulled reservation bill requiring east coast LNG exporters to reserve up to 20% of gas output for domestic use from 2028, aiming to ease supply shortages and price pressure while leaving Western Australia’s 15% policy intact.
Houthi Strike Ras Tanura Again. Yemen’s Houthi militias claimed a successful hit on Saudi Arabia’s 550,000 b/d Ras Tanura refinery, with satellite imagery showing two storage tanks fully burnt down, though Saudi authorities did not confirm any damage as the impact on fuel output remained unclear.
Lukoil’s Assets Have Finally Found a Buyer. US billionaire Todd Boehly announced that his consortium (backed by Trump’s US DFC investment arm), had signed a $10 billion securities swap for Lukoil’s overseas assets, giving Washington a share of future profits but still requiring US Treasury approval.
The Blame Game Outlasts COP31. OPEC Secretary General Haitham Al Ghais blamed the EU for the collapse of the COP31 talks in Antalya, accusing Brussels of double standards after it delayed methane reporting for fuel importers while rejecting a deal that omitted a transition away from fossil fuels.
Ukraine Keeps on Droning Russian Refineries. Ukraine struck the 70,000 b/d Slavyansk ECO refinery this week, seriously damaging the main crude distillation unit and associated storage tanks, threatening to delay a restart at a plant already offline for repairs after an earlier September attack.
Green Fuel Hits Turbulence. The European Commission opened an anti-dumping probe into sustainable aviation fuel (SAF) from China and Singapore, raising the prospect of retroactive duties in a market where Chinese producers are estimated to supply more than 60% of European demand this year.
Jakarta’s Cheap Fuel Comes at a Price. The Indonesian government is reportedly considering raising subsidised fuel prices for the first time in five years, with a possible hike in early 2027 as high oil prices and a weak rupiah push this year’s energy subsidy bill to an estimated $27.2 billion, 30% above budget.
Turkey Expands Its Upstream Push to Pakistan. Pakistan and Turkey outlined a joint offshore exploration programme to identify new oil and gas resources in the South Asian nation, with a Turkish seismic survey vessel set to assess 670 km 2 of the Indus basin to identify drilling targets for 2027.
Japanese Carmakers Are Losing China. Global sales of Japanese carmaker Toyota (TYO:7203) fell 6.3% year-on-year to 940,809 vehicles in October, marking a ninth straight monthly decline as the firm posted a whopping 25% slump in China, only partially offset by a hybrid-led 6.5% gain in the US.
Key Bangkok Refinery Hits the Pause Button. Thai refiner Bangchak shut all production units at its 120,000 b/d Phra Khanong refinery after a fire engulfed the plant this week, immediately seeking diesel imports from neighbouring countries as the damaged plant supplies most of Thailand’s capital.
Moscow Grounds Its Jet Fuel Exports. Russia extended its ban on jet fuel exports through 31 March 2027 to protect domestic supply after refinery strikes cut processing rates, though seaborne exports were already low at 25,000 b/d and shipments under intergovernmental agreements remain exempt.
The World’s First Lithium Hydroxide Futures Falter. The Guangzhou Futures Exchange launched lithium hydroxide futures on Thursday, with the most-traded June 2027 contract immediately sliding more than 7% below its starting price at 69,600 yuan a tonne ($10,440 per tonne) amidst weak battery demand.

articles.title_orig: EU budget summit ends abruptly in Brussels
articles.title_zh: EU budget summit ends abruptly in Brussels
articles.content_orig:
EU leaders arrived in Brussels braced for a difficult showdown over the bloc's multitrillion-euro seven-year budget. But few expected the summit to unravel so quickly, with talks breaking down late on Thursday night.
Squabbles and thinly veiled public barbs meant they left without a deal and didn't even attempt to resume discussions on the planned second day.
There is a self-imposed deadline to find agreement before the end of 2026 on the budget which covers the 2028-2034 period. But experts say there is no cause for alarm, yet.
"Every time there are long-term EU budget negotiations, there are breakdowns, chaos, recrimination and a lot of political theater and drama," said Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, an EU economist and expert at the Bruegel think tank in Brussels.
The center of that political theater this time was the prime ministers of Denmark, Sweden, Belgium and Austria — countries wanting a reduced budget — who staged a walkout during smaller, group meetings, claiming the atmosphere had not been constructive to getting a deal.
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar called the whole summit "completely unnecessary," pointing the blame at the man who had decided to call it and whose job it is to meditate the talks, European Council President Antonio Costa.
Costa was diplomatic in defending his decision to bring the leaders to Brussels, telling the press: "For me it was very useful to figure out the parameters of a possible landing zone in December."
Long before the summit started, Germany had laid down an ultimatum — Berlin would only sign off on the budget if all the other EU countries greenlit an additional €45 billion ($49 billion) support loan for Ukraine to fund the country in its war efforts through 2027.
Hungary, Czechia, Bulgaria and Slovakia have dug their heels in against the proposal, insisting that giving Ukraine money to buy weapons will prolong the war. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico even accused Germany of "blackmail."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
As Europe's biggest economy, Germany's contribution amounts to around 25% of the whole budget.
In a press conference after the summit, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said "hundreds of billions" still need to be slashed. The European Commission's original proposal of approximately €1.786 trillion had already been reduced by €204 billion (down 10.2%).
"Europe needs to exercise a sense of proportion," said Merz. "The budget cannot grow indefinitely, and the burden of financing it must be distributed fairly."
Merz also aimed a comment toward Costa, who has been renewing the details in the budget proposal at every stage.
"The proposals that have been on the table so far are not a basis for an agreement," said Merz.
Costa did tell leaders on Thursday that he is planning to cut between €220 billion to €230 billion out of the next proposal.
Berlin's budget reduction push is backed by six other countries who together call themselves the "Sensible Seven." All pay more into the collective EU financial pot than they receive out of it.
They are opposed by 17 EU member states who insist the total budget should grow, led by France and Italy. These countries call themselves the "Friends of Cohesion" — a nod to the EU cohesion funds which are used to share wealth from the EU's richer regions and nations to its poorer ones.
In the current proposal, agriculture, fisheries and cohesion spending falls from 59.1% to 42.4%, while money for economic competitiveness, security, and defense rises from 17.7% to 27.7%. This rebalancing is a key German demand.
The EU is also searching for a way to add money into the budget that doesn't come from national contributions. The current proposal includes a controversial EU-wide digital tax which could chart a course for a major battle with the US.
The idea, originally put forward by French President Emmanuel Macron, is for a 3% tax on revenues of online advertising, online marketplaces and on the monetization of user data. The money, to be paid directly into the EU's budget, is estimated to bring in €5 billion per year.
But the proposal is ringing alarm bells in Ireland, where US tech giants like Google, Meta, Apple, Microsoft and LinkedIn have their European headquarters.
"A digital tax is sending out all the wrong messages," said Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin, who could still veto the proposal.
There is a fear in some European capitals that without being able to generate its own funds, future EU loans could downgrade the European Commission's unblemished standing on international markets.
The EU has around €860 billion in outstanding debts it took out for its pandemic recovery funding and to support Ukraine. Its triple-A credit rating could be downgraded if Marine Le Pen , the far-right front-runner in France's presidential election, wins in the spring and follows through on her promise to reduce French contributions to the EU budget.
EU member states that favor a financing model through national contributions rather than through tax revenue "understand very well what will happen if the EU loses its triple-A rating," said Bruegel's Kirkegaard. "Interest rate costs will go up even more. Who has to pay for that? Net contributing countries, like Germany, the Nordics, the Dutch, which is why they are much more open to this than in the past."
Other European tax experts believe that prior examples of these digital taxes show the costs outweigh the benefits.
"We analyzed the states which have a digital services tax [DST], and we've seen that economic cost exceeds the revenue generated," said Cristina Enache, an economist at the Brussels-based nonprofit Tax Foundation Europe. "Spain has a DST and the expected revenue was twice or three times larger than what they actually are collecting."
Enache called the tax proposal "politically impossible."
EU leaders know that the clock on their end-of-2026 deadline is ticking, and will return to the same conference rooms in late December hoping for a more conducive atmosphere to strike a deal.

articles.title_orig: Mélenchon takes aim at Germany in Berlin campaign stop
articles.title_zh: Mélenchon takes aim at Germany in Berlin campaign stop
articles.content_orig:
PARIS — It’s an unusual way to prepare for a trip to Berlin: suggesting Germany might pose a military threat to your country.
But that’s exactly what French presidential contender Jean-Luc Mélenchon did ahead of his visit this week.
“I’m not ok with Germany’s pledge to build the largest conventional army in Europe,” the far-left leader said earlier this month, on Armistice Day, a holiday that in France commemorates the end of the intense fighting between France and Germany in World War I. “Because if it does, I have to ask: Who does it want to go to war against?”
The comments up the ante on Mélenchon’s long-standing defiance toward France’s neighbor, which he accuses of acting as a hegemon in Europe. His hostility toward Berlin — part longtime obsession, part political positioning — is one of the many ways the far-left leader clashes with his country’s establishment, which has traditionally worked closely with Berlin to shape the continent.
Unsurprisingly, his comments have riled many in Germany, given that the rearmament effort was a response to Russia’s 2022 full-scale invasion of Ukraine.
“Mélenchon paints a distorted picture of Germany and Franco-German relations,” said Roland Theis, a German lawmaker from the conservative Christian Democratic Union who chairs the Bundestag’s Franco-German Parliamentary Group and sits on its Defense Committee.
The leftist veteran is polling in second place ahead of next year’s presidential election, putting him within reach of a runoff against the far-right front-runner, Marine Le Pen. For some in Berlin, neither prospect is particularly reassuring.
“On security and European affairs, his political positions are at least as dangerous as Le Pen’s,” Theis said.
A critic of Berlin’s traditional positions on fiscal and European affairs, Mélenchon is the author of a 2015 book subtitled “The German Poison.”
His France Unbowed party has long criticized joint Franco-German defense projects, arguing they favor German interests at the expense of French defense companies. The party also mistrusts the United States — Mélenchon has pledged to leave NATO — and his lieutenants have described Berlin as Washington’s “Trojan Horse” in Europe.
He intends to double down on his criticisms at an event in Berlin on Friday night, where he will present a German translation of another book: “Now, the People! — Revolution in the 21st Century,” which lays out his vision for France, Europe and the world.
In his presidential platform, Mélenchon pledged to radically overhaul the EU , disobeying its rules if necessary.
“We are being honest,” said Hadrien Clouet, a lawmaker from Mélenchon’s France Unbowed who will accompany him to Germany. “We have to say what we think: Chancellor [Friedrich] Merz is a problem for Europe.”
The event is being organized with the support of the Rosa Luxemburg Foundation, which is affiliated with Germany’s far-left Left Party. Mélenchon is expected to meet privately with party representatives Saturday.
Aurélien Taché, the party’s point person on the French National Assembly’s foreign affairs committee, said Mélenchon’s problem wasn’t with the German people.
“We think there is a very strong German influence [in Europe], with an ordoliberal vision that we strongly reject,” Taché said. Concerns about hybrid warfare by Russia “don’t justify recreating a Wehrmacht as Europe’s leading military power,” Taché said, using the German word for Nazis’ armed forces.
While Mélenchon has taken his antipathy toward Berlin further than any other leading French politician, doubts around the Franco-German relationship aren’t limited to the far end of the political spectrum.
In a poll published this month and conducted by the French branch of the European think tank More in Common in July, 71% of respondents described Germany as an ally. While that was more than any other international partner, it was down 6 percentage points from last year, led by a sharp drop among conservatives, traditionally among the most pro-German part of the electorate.
Even mainstream French politicians have begun to temper their enthusiasm for Franco-German industrial cooperation after Germany decided unilaterally to pull the plug on a joint effort to design and build a next-generation fighter jet and in the face of cooled support by Berlin for a similar project for tanks.
Leading center-right candidates such as Edouard Philippe, a German speaker, have said that Paris should look beyond Berlin to form new partnerships and beef up its security. Le Pen, who has long shared Mélenchon’s defiance, said on Thursday she wanted to end the era of “German Europe.”
“German rearmament strikes a chord historically for many voters,” said Paul Maurice, an expert on Franco-German relations at the French Institute of International Relations. “It speaks to the collective psyche.”
Beyond security fears, German defense spending also plays on French insecurities as the country grapples with a prolonged public finances crisis.
“When [voters] look at Germany today, they see what France is not capable of doing any more,” Maurice said. Tellingly, he added, “Mélenchon is the first candidate to go to Berlin” during the campaign.
And, so far, the only one.
CLARIFICATION: This article was updated on Nov. 26 to clarify when the More in Common poll was conducted. It was conducted in July.

articles.title_orig: Like clockwork, the Pixel 11 is a way better buy after a few months [Video]
articles.title_zh: Like clockwork, the Pixel 11 is a way better buy after a few months [Video]
articles.content_orig:
If you've been holding off on picking up one of Google's latest smartphones in the hopes that you'd see some good deals this Black Friday, then you are in luck. Google has discounted several of its latest Pixel devices as part of its Black Friday sale, with the unlocked Pixel 11 dropping from $899 to just $699. And if you're willing to switch wireless providers, you can actually get your hands on the Pixel 11 without paying anything for the phone itself beyond the applicable taxes.
The deal, which is available through the Google Store , lets you save the entire retail price of the Pixel 11 when you sign up for Google Fi Wireless. Google is also offering a discount on its most expensive unlimited wireless plan, allowing you to save an additional $240 over the course of two years. And, unlike many smartphone deals you'll probably see this Black Friday, you don't even need to trade in your old phone to take advantage of the savings.
Considering the Pixel 11 is only a few months old and comes with twice the starting storage of its predecessor, as well as some improvements to its camera system, it's a particularly enticing offer, although Google does play it a bit too safe with the Pixel 11 . Of course, as is often the case with these types of carrier deals, there are a few caveats you'll want to familiarize yourself with before pulling the trigger.
To take advantage of the deal, you'll need to be a new Google Fi Wireless customer and select Google Fi as your carrier when purchasing the Pixel 11 through the Google Store. You'll receive an immediate $300 discount on the smartphone, with the remaining $599 distributed across 24 monthly bill credits. You'll also need to activate the smartphone within 30 days of receiving confirmation that it has shipped.
The biggest caveat here, though, is that you'll need to remain with Google Fi Wireless for two years to take full advantage of the promotion. Canceling or pausing your service, or changing your plan prematurely, will result in you forfeiting the remaining promotional credits. Additionally, switching to another smartphone within the first 120 days will result in Google charging you for that initial $300 discount.
It's also worth noting that Google is offering a similar promotion for the Pixel 11 Pro, covering the entirety of that smartphone's $1,099 starting price. As such, if you've been debating whether to buy the Pixel 11 or the Pixel 11 Pro , this particular promotion makes a pretty compelling argument for going with Google's more premium smartphone instead. The deal is available until January 5, 2027, or while supplies last, so you don't necessarily have to rush out and buy the Pixel 11 on Black Friday itself.
While switching wireless providers just to get a free smartphone might not always make sense, Google Fi is one of several affordable wireless carriers that utilize T-Mobile's network in the United States. So if you have good T-Mobile coverage in your area, then it could be a good move. On top of the deal, if you sign up for Google's Unlimited Premium plan alongside your new Pixel 11, you'll pay $55 a month instead of the usual $65 for the first two years.
The Unlimited Premium plan includes 100 GB of high-speed data per person each month, 50 GB of high-speed hotspot data, and international data coverage in more than 200 destinations. Google also throws in 100 GB of Google One cloud storage and six months of YouTube Premium. If you're already paying around $55 or more a month for your wireless service, then switching could essentially net you a new flagship smartphone without increasing your monthly spending.
If two years of bill credits isn't enough to convince you to change, then you can always take advantage of another deal that Google has to offer. Purchasing an unlocked Pixel smartphone through the Google Store will actually qualify you for 12 months of complimentary Google Fi Unlimited Essentials service, or you can receive an equivalent discount toward one of the carrier's more expensive unlimited plans.
